Mr. Speaker, once again I rise to present petitions signed by Canadians who are concerned about the future of the Port of Churchill.
The Port of Churchill is crucial to the health of the economy of the prairie provinces. Already, the result of the reduced grain shipments through Churchill is beginning to show. subtopic: CUSTOMS TARIFF
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on Bill C-17, an Act to amend the Customs Tariff. This Bill does several things, largely administrative in nature, but it makes certain amendments to eliminate the tariff on certain goods which are not produced in Canada, to change to some degree some of the remission orders, and to remove duties from certain products such as time recorders, vessels for scrapping, and checking fixtures imported temporarily for manufacturing production equipment.
Duty is also reduced on low alcohol beer, and excise and duty sales taxes are raised to align the treatment of imported lower alcohol beer into line with domestic beer. It also extends the authority to restore the pre-har-monized system tariff rates. In large part, the Bill is administrative in nature. We have no objections to those sections.
One section of the Bill deals with customs tariff prohibition on pornographic, hate, treasonable, and seditious materials. On December 31, 1989 the current regulation is scheduled to expire. This Bill proposes that no longer will it be necessary for annual review of this section in Parliament. In 1985 when this section was implemented as the result of a court case, it was decided that it was important that Parliament have a chance to review this particular amendment on an annual basis.
Since that time, through the Ministry of Justice, there have been Bills presented to the House, which have not gone through owing to the election last fall, to deal with the more serious issue of the definition of pornographic and seditious material, hate literature, and so on.
The customs Department and its officers find themselves making decisions based on an ill-defined definition of materials upon which they have to make judgments. In the Salman Rushdie The Satanic Verses
Customs Tariff
case, customs officers made a decision to withhold the importation of that book for several days based on an interpretation of this particular Act. That then led to a fairly large controversy on the ability of customs officers to make those choices on the law as it stands. Clause 25 of the Bill is not highly explanatory and states:
Code 9956 in Schedule VII to the said Act is amended by striking
out the words following paragraph (d) thereof.
Basically that means that rather than having to come back to Parliament on an annual basis to discuss this issue and to seek further extension, it will be included in the Act for an indefinite period of time.
We raised this question in 1985 when it was originally instituted, and we still have considerable problems with it. Admittedly, much of the problem rests with the Ministry of Justice having to define this and to set the policy. Customs Tariff obviously implements the policy and makes the decisions. However, the responsibility for the definition rests with the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lewis). This is a major unfinished piece of business. The Criminal Code must be examined in relation to this area.
As I stated, there continues to be a problem in this area. There was the recent case to which I referred concerning the Salman Rushdie book. We do not know what other cases may arise of a similar nature. The place that this must be addressed is within the Criminal Code by the Ministry of Justice.
However, this time it is not going forward, at least in this session of Parliament it would appear, and for that reason we will oppose the Bill based on Clause 25 specifically, because of our concern that until this issue is clarified in the Criminal Code it should come before Parliament on an annual basis for review.

subtopic: NATIONAL ENERGY BOARD ACT

speechtext:
Hon. Jean Charest (for Minister of Energy, Mines and
Resources) moved that Bill C-23, an Act to amend the National Energy Board Act and to repeal certain enactments in consequence thereof, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

subtopic: NATIONAL ENERGY BOARD ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am rather disappointed that the Government has not seen fit to have someone from its side to introduce this Bill, particularly since this is second reading.
It is a very important Bill, although the Government would have us believe differently. The Government describes Bill C-23 more or less as a Bill to do some housecleaning points with respect to the National Energy Board. I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that it is a great deal more than just a few housekeeping points with respect to the National Energy Board.
Bill C-23 has tremendously far-reaching implications for our country. It will change dramatically the way in which we will allow exports of electricity from our producing provinces into the United States. To a large extent it will affect the regulations and the conditions under which consuming provinces will be able to receive electricity from the producing provinces.
June 26, 1989

In the past we have had certain rules and regulations, a strong presence in the National Energy Board, regarding this point. I think the system has worked quite well. With respect to the National Energy Board, we are also making some changes to the Board itself. We are getting a few significant changes with respect to the export of oil and gas from Canada into the United States and presumably other countries, if we are going to be in a position to sell oil to other countries.
I think the major issue here is electricity. The Government has altered drastically the means by which we are going to export electricity into the United States and the conditions under which we can assure our interconnecting utilities, that is, other provinces connected to the producing provinces, of at least a portion of the electricity from the producing provinces at a comparable price.
To begin I would like to talk about the situation as it was which gave the National Energy Board a veiy strong presence. The Board, which was first recommended by the Borden Commission in 1958, has been a marvellous organization which has served the country extremely well. Even today the National Energy Board is comprised of very competent individuals. They have done the job that has been asked of them extremely well. I think it is one of our best agencies.
First and foremost the National Energy Board has had the jurisdiction to approve or to turn down the export of oil and gas and electricity into the United States. With respect to electricity there were certain guidelines under which the Board operated.
The first was that the producing provinces had to be able to pay the cost of producing the electricity before the Board would allow it to be exported, something which makes a great deal of sense. Also, the producing province had to include in its cost of production certain indirect effects of that production. The foremost effect was environmental. If there were environmental effects as a result of the production of electricity then, of course, there would be a cost not only to the producing province, but a cost to the federal Government as well, which should be compensated for in the price of electricity. That is to say, the price should be able to allow for the reimbursement of the province and the citizens of the province the cost of producing that electricity, and the cost of bringing back the environment as much as
National Energy Board
possible to the state it was before the actual production of electricity took place.
The second point is that if it was being sold into the United States it could not be sold below the least cost alternative. That is to say the National Energy Board insisted that if we are going to sell electricity to the United States it could not be below the cost of the other form of energy which was the cheapest in the United States. For instance, if natural gas was cheaper than all other fuels in the U.S., then the price of electricity, the comparable energy value of electricity, could not be cheaper. It could not be sold more cheaply into the U.S. than the equivalent of the cost of natural gas.
Third, if electricity were to be sold into the U.S. then interconnecting utilities, in particular other provinces, had the right to make application to the National Energy Board to have at least a portion of that electricity sold at a comparable price. This was considered fair for two reasons, the first being that it would be natural to assume that we would first look after the interests of other provinces in Canada before we looked after the interests of foreign countries.
Some of the other provinces, and I think in particular of the smallest province, Prince Edward Island, was absolutely dependent upon getting its electricity from Quebec through New Brunswick, which made that province very vulnerable. With that in mind, the Board protected all the provinces to ensure that they were looked after in that regard and that the price for which the electricity would be sold to these other provinces would be the same as it would be sold in the United States, thereby not creating hardship for the producing province. Of course, there would be different cost depending upon the cost of transmission of the electricity. If it went to a province that was farther away than the American market, of course it would be more expensive to that province because of the transportation charges. That was a benefit for all of Canada and was considered to be a very strongly held principle by the former Liberal Government.
However, there were some objections which I think have to be looked at and considered. Some of the producing provinces were concerned, and I think with some justification, that if they sold to interconnecting utilities then those utilities in turn would sell that electricity into the United States at a higher price, thereby making a profit for electricity that was not theirs. All they would have done was take it from one province and sell it into the United States, thereby making a sizeable sum of money on electricity which was gener-

June 26, 1989
National Energy Board
ated in another province. That made the generating provinces somewhat upset, which I think is understandable. It was something that was in the forefront of the Government's mind when it brought forward this legislation. While it has dealt with this, in doing so it has created many problems within the Bill itself.
This legislation is not suitable for the country. It is a cop out on the role of the federal Government on its responsibility to Canada. It is abandoning its role with respect to jurisdiction over the export of electricity and control of the environment to allow the provinces to do what they want.
Of course, there are provincial laws with respect to energy. Electricity, perhaps more than other forms of energy, lies within provincial jurisdiction. That has always been recognized and must continue to be recognized. The provinces have their own responsibilities and jurisdiction.
Bill C-23 is an Act to amend the National Energy Board Act, but as I said earlier, it is considerably more than that. Clause 58.19 states:
For the purposes of sections 58.2, 58.21 and 58.22, a law of a province is in relation to lines for the transmission of electricity from a place in the province to another place in the province if the law is in relation to any of the following matters;
One consideration is:
(c) assessments of their impact on the environment;
This is, to be solely within the jurisdiction of the province. Transmission from one part of the province to another part of the province, and concerns regarding the environment, are a provincial concern. That is not overly disturbing because the province will have to take responsibility for any decisions regarding transmission lines that are offensive environmentally within that province.
Clause 119.06 deals with licences and the export of electricity to the United States. It states:
(2) In deciding whether to make a recommendation, the Board shall have regard to all considerations that appear to it to be relevant, including-
(b)	whether the exportation of the electricity would result in the contravention of or failure to comply with environmental requirements of the Government of Canada;
I will return to that clause later, but the point I want to make is that the Government has addressed the transmission of electricity from one part of the province to another part of the same province, as the responsibility of the Department of the Environment of the province, and the export of electricity to be the jurisdiction of the federal Government, but the Bill does not deal with the interprovincial sale of electricity. There is nothing in the Bill dealing with who has control over problems with the environment when electricity is sold from one province to another. This major omission has been brought to the attention of the Government but it has not dealt with it.
Rather than making a simple omission, I believe the Government has done this intentionally. Let me refer to a speech made by the former Minister of Energy, the Minister of Communications (Mr. Masse) in 1988. He
said:
It is inevitable that provincial regulations will be applied to the determination of the detailed routing for international power lines. National Energy Board regulation of the detailed route is hence unnecessary except, perhaps in the case of a line traversing more than one provinces that is not supported by all of the provinces in which it will pass.
He made that point in his speech but there is nothing in the Bill to deal with that matter. He went on to say:
The detailed routing and land acquisition provisions of the National Energy Board Act will therefore not apply to international power lines except when: (i) the line passes through more than one province; and (ii) a sponsoring province so requests.
Even though a licence for routing power lines is extraterritorial as far as Canada is concerned, the former Minister said that the federal Government can only take into consideration the environmental questions when a line passes through more than one province and when the sponsoring province so requests. That is completely unacceptable, particularly when one considers the importance of environmental factors today and the attention being given to the environment by Canadians today.
The Minister went on to say:
June 26, 1989

The Government of Canada will now seek to develop-
That is within the legislation before us today:
- in co-operation with the provinces and the electrical industry, environmental guidelines and standards applicable to electricity generation and transmission. The goal would be a co-ordinated nation-wide effort designed to achieve a consensus on environmental norms, while providing flexibility on how these norms are to be adapted to local circumstances and on how they are to be achieved.
There is no consensus in this legislation. There is no consensus brought before us in the House today. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Epp) will tell us that the consensus exists, but to my knowledge and according to my information, no consensus has been reached between the provinces on the one hand and the federal Government on the other.
Let me turn to Clause 58.29(4). It states:
The appropriate authority may grant leave under this section after construction of the proposed work has commenced if the appropriate authority is satisfied that the work was urgently required and, prior to the commencement of construction, the appropriate authority was notified of the intention of the holder of the permit or certificate issued in respect of the line to proceed with the proposed work.
I suggest this actually encourages the start-up of construction of power lines before approval is given. The Government is acting irresponsibly in making such an insinuation.
Clause 58.39 states:
The Governor in Council may make regulations for carrying into effect the purposes and provisions of this Part, including regulations-
Let me illustrate some of the stipulations of the regulations:
(a)	prescribing matters in respect of which terms and conditions of permits may be imposed:
(b)	respecting the information to be furnished in connection with applications for permits:
(c)	specifying considerations to which the Board shall have regard in deciding whether to recommend to the Minister that an international power line be designated by order of the Governor in Council under Section 58.15; and
(d)	prescribing the form of elections filed under Section 58.23.
This brings us to a very important point regarding this legislation. Regardless of the fact that it has many clauses, it is merely shell legislation. The Government has intentionally made the Bill so innocuous, bland and ineffective that we cannot say what it will accomplish
National Energy Board
unless we have a complete list of the regulations before us.
The legislation is very indefinite and uncertain, yet we are being asked to comment on and approve it at second reading. The Bill is too sketchy. What the Government is doing of course, having intentionally made the Bill as sketchy as it possibly can, is trying to bring in after the Bill is passed the meat of the whole process of the export of electricity in regulations.
I would like to go to what I consider perhaps the key to this Bill. How are we going to regulate the export of electricity into the United States? This Government has come through with a novel concept. It talks about permits and licences. You can export electricity based on licences or you can export electricity based on permits.
If you read the Act, it does not give you a great deal of information other than to say that the National Energy Board can agree to the export of electricity into the United States via a permit without a Board hearing. That is, the National Energy Board will decide if it wants to allow the export of electricity from any province of Canada into the United States and give a permit for this export, but there will be no hearing involved. That means that there is no way really that we have a chance to get the full disclosure of the actual export.
Then it goes one step further and says that if the National Energy Board feels that there should be a hearing, which is the National Energy Board's right and which it has done up to the present time very effectively-albeit some applications have taken a long time to be approved, but that could be remedied with changes in procedure-but it can give a permit without a hearing. However, if the National Energy Board finds that there should be a hearing, they have to make this recommendation to the Governor in Council. The Governor in Council decides whether there should be a hearing or not.
Therefore, it really is not the National Energy Board that is controlling the export of electricity, it is the Governor in Council and the federal Government. It decides, be it for political reasons, leverage or whatever, without giving any kind of answer or explanation as to why, whether there is going to be a review or not. If there is a hearing or a review and the review is approved, then of course there is a licence issued. If the Governor in

June 26, 1989
National Energy Board
Council says no, there is not to be a hearing, then the permit is given.
This is a complete abdication of the principles of review that have been so important in dealing with Canada's energy self-sufficiency and the export of energy into the United States. I do not doubt that the sale of electricity is very important to the provinces. I frankly do not see many reasons that exist for denying applications, but still it is a federal responsibility. It is a federal responsibility, but Canadians have the right to look at the applications and get some idea of what it is that the Government is doing by way of commerce with the United States.
The Free Trade Agreement has already ruled out the second rule of thumb. That is, that energy can only be sold into the United States at no less a price than the least cost alternative. The Government seems to be saying in this Bill that the price is purely within the realm and jurisdiction of the province and that it does not want to interfere in the provincial domain regardless of whether the domain in which the provincial government is acting is a federal domain or not. What the federal Government is saying is, if the provincial Government has made regulations, the federal Government should not interfere. It is a travesty of the rights of Canadians. It is a travesty as far as this Government's responsibility to fulfil its role in the export of energy into the United States.
Just let me give an example from that same speech that the then Minister of Energy made in September of 1988. He said:
As I have already noted, this regulatory approach does not explicitly take account the fact that Canadian utilities are already comprehensively regulated by the provinces. The new policy does. It can be summarized very briefly.
Four of the points that he makes in his summary are:
Approval will be by permit, except in those cases designated by the Governor-in-Council. Permits will not require a public hearing or a review by the Governor-in-Council.
The Governor-in-Council may designate an export for licensing or a power line for certification if there is any reason to believe that regulation by the sponsoring province is insufficient.
Designations will be made on the advice of the Board, and such advice will be made public.
Proposals that have been designated by the Governor-in-Council will be reviewed by the NEB through the public-hearing process. In considering the application, the Board will have regard to all relevant matters.
The reference to all relevant matters will be the matters set down in the directive of the Governor in Council in the regulations which we do not have at the present time and dealing with the licensing of the application that really the Governor in Council will dictate, not the National Energy Board.
I want to look at another point which I think is very important. At that time, approximately September 2, 1988, we have an example of what the Government of Canada was looking at in a letter to Mr. R. Priddle, Chairman of the National Energy Board. The former Minister of Energy said:
Where appropriate, the Governor-in-Council may designate exports and international power lines for licensing or certification procedures. Once designated, an application will be considered by the Board through a public-hearing process and any authorization will require Govemor-in-Council approval.
It is very strongly stated that there is not to be a hearing unless the Governor in Council says that there is going to be a hearing. With this whole realm of abandoning the responsibility over jurisdiction of exports of energy, and particularly in this case, electricity, we cannot see this Government actually requiring a hearing in any situation.
The former Minister of Energy, the present Minister of Communications goes on to say:
Designations will occur in instances where there is reason to believe that provincial review procedures are insufficient for determining whether a proposal is in the Canadian public interest.
What provincial review procedures? Today the provinces get a contract and they sell. Those are the review procedures, and to say that the review procedures are not sufficient really does not differ one case from another. As I have said, we are just going to have a complete abdication of responsibility by the federal Government in this regard.
Where we had the most concern, and this is something to which I alluded earlier, was whether the interconnecting utilities would be affected by the sale of electricity into the United States. There is considerable progress to be made in that regard. Subsection (2) of Section 119.06 says:
June 26, 1989

In deciding whether to make a recommendation, the Board shall have regard to all considerations that appear to it to be relevant, including -
(c)(i) informs those who have declared an interest in buying electricity for consumption in Canada of the quantities and classes of services available for sale, and
(ii) given an opportunity to purchase electricity on terms and conditions as favourable as the terms and conditions specified in the application of those who, within a reasonable time after being so informed, demonstrate an intention to buy electricity for consumption in Canada-
There are a couple of things there which I think are important. First, the province that buys the electricity from the exporting province must show that that electricity is going to be consumed in Canada. That is easy for a province such as Prince Edward Island because Prince Edward Island is not in the position to export electricity. However, when provinces generate electricity from coal, nuclear power, or perhaps co-generation, how do we determine which electricity that second province would in turn export into the United States in breach of this provision?
There has to be some determination by the National Energy Board of who would be breaching that guideline. We cannot put the burden of proof back on the province that buys it. If the words "the purchasing province, within a reasonable time after being so informed, demonstrate an intention to buy electricity for the consumption in Canada" are questioned, it then becomes an argument between the two provinces.
The other question is when this electricity agreement has to be entered into. What if there are disagreements and that struggle drags on and on? Who then has the power to intercede? I think that there are questions which are not going to be healthy in the dealings between one province and another.
I would like to point out as well that there is a tremendous amount of latitude with the Governor in Council and I want to mention again that there are two systems. The National Energy Board can issue a permit without an investigation, but if it wants an investigation it has to ask the permission of the Governor in Council. Permission is given under Clause 119.07 which says:
The Governor in Council may make orders
National Energy Board
(a)	designating an exportation of electricity as an exportation that is
subject to the issuance of a licence under section 119.08;
(b)	specifying considerations to which the Board shall have regard
in deciding whether to issue such a licence; and
(c)	revoking any permit issued in respect of the exportation.
Therefore, if the National Energy Board wants to have a hearing it has to get approval from the Governor in Council. The Governor in Council not only says whether or not the hearing will be approved but, if it is approved by the very Act itself, the Governor in Council specifies considerations to which the Board shall have regard in deciding whether to issue such a licence. That takes all the power away from the National Energy Board, the agency which was set up by a former Government of Canada to regulate the export of electricity and oil and gas into the United States.
We have come a long way in reducing the powers of the National Energy Board. We did so, of course, through the Free Trade Agreement, and we are going to do so again through this Bill. We are going to have to study this Bill very carefully.
One thing of which I am glad with regard to Bill C-23 is that it will not be going to committee until the fall when we will have a chance to question at length officials and the Minister regarding these provisions.
It is also important to talk to the National Energy Board and the various provinces to get their opinions. We are going to have to take a very hard look at this. We also say in this Bill, with respect to oil and gas, that the Board does have the power to regulate price in the sale of oil and gas, except in the case of the United States.
I am wondering if this may not be the start of a continental energy policy with the United States. The Government says not; it says that the Free Trade Agreement does not give a continental energy policy. In fact, the Government, quite correctly, still has the power to assure that energy not be sold into the United States at a price cheaper than that at which that form of energy is available in Canada. However, if that provision holds in this Bill and the Government abandons all authority and all provision for regulating any price at which energy is sold into the United States, we will have in fact entered into a continental energy policy with the United States.

June 26, 1989
National Energy Board
This Bill is a real problem for this House. It is going to be a problem for Canada. It is going to be a further abdication of federal government responsibility, which the Government does better than anything else it takes on. I hope that we can give this Bill a full study. I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that we will not be agreeing to this Bill until some very significant changes have been made.

subtopic: NATIONAL ENERGY BOARD ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as my hon. friend has already mentioned, there are a number of interesting, if somewhat arcane aspects to Bill C-23, all of which are worthy of some attention.
I would like to devote my remarks today to those parts of the Bill which deal with its principal goals, the guts of the Bill which seek, simply put, to make it easier for provincial jurisdictions to export electrical power to the United States of America. However, before getting into those particulars I would like, if I may, to take a few minutes to review the history of electric production and regulation in Canada in capsule form.
The Canadian electrical industry has long been subject to regulation at both the provincial and federal levels. This is largely for historic reasons. The industry began as a collection of small hydraulic plants serving isolated loads at the beginning of the century and developed into a vast interconnected network that now spans the country. Because provincial power networks were developed in isolation, and because electricity service was commonly viewed as an essential prerequisite to economic development, individual provinces were keen to retain the exclusive jurisdiction that the Constitution Act had given them in 1867 over what was then termed the "development, conservation and management of sites and facilities in the province for the generation and production of electrical energy".
Not surprisingly, given the monopoly position of many electrical utilities, most provinces eventually decided to place electrical utilities under provincial ownership or, at very least, under close provincial control in terms of rates charged to consumers and satisfying the province's needs and export commitments.
In my Province of Alberta we have, for example, the Public Utilities Board, the principal government agency overseeing the electrical industry. We have as well the
Energy Resources Conservation Board which has some jurisdiction in the area and, most recently, the Electrical Energy Marketing Agency which is the provincially created agency for the pooling of electricity rates charged to Albertans. I believe we still have, however, four power companies operating in Alberta, two of which are publicly owned.
The provinces thus have interests that cover both provincial concerns and concerns of export, and these interests are those which often overlap with federal interests. In fact, this overlap was virtually guaranteed by that same Constitution Act, 1867 which granted authority over international trade and commerce to the federal Parliament.
As a result, the regulation of electricity exports and the regulation of international power lines clearly fall within federal jurisdiction. The regulation of the electricity industry in Canada has reflected the growth and evolution both of the industry and the country itself. Industry has long been regulated by both the provinces and the federal Government. This has been a fact of Canadian life.
The federal Government, from the outset, attempted to ensure that any exports of electricity were surplus to Canadian needs. This has really been the hallmark of federal policy for decades. In fact, even prior to the establishment of the National Energy Board in 1959, export prices were reviewed and exports were regulated to make sure that hydro-electric resources would not be alienated from Canadians. This focus persisted after the Royal Commission on Energy recommended the formation of the NEB. As the then Minister of Trade and Commerce, the Hon. Gordon Churchill, put it in 1959:
In the case of electricity, it has been the policy in the past to grant only annual licences for export, so as to prevent permanent alienation of power.
The National Energy Board Act of 1959 extended the maximum export licence period from one to 25 years, but there was a clear expectation that long-term licences would be granted only in exceptional circumstances. As the National Energy Board report of 1987 put it:
The rationale-appears to have been that, if Canadian energy were to be sold to export customers at prices lower than those at which it were sold to Canadians, it would undermine the competitive position of Canadian industry vis-a-vis its American competitors and be unfair to Canadian consumers.
June 26, 1989

I think it worth while to recall what the then Prime Minister, the Right Hon. John George Diefenbaker, a fine and historic western leader who was possessed of a great wisdom to which this House should still pay heed, said when the details of the NEB Act were debated in Parliament in 1959. He outlined what had been the preoccupation of federal policy for years. In referring to the NEB Act of 1959, he said:
As to the price to be charged for gas and power, it must be just and reasonable in relation to the public interest. With the implementation of this legislation.
No longer will there be any suspicion that the Canadian consumer is being forced to subsidize the foreign markets or that Canadian industries will be asked to pay higher prices for their energy than those paid by foreign industries using Canadian energy - The Bill protects not only the industrial future of Canada but the producer and the consumer.
The statement of national power policy released in 1962 by the then Minister of Trade and Commerce, the Hon. Mitchell Sharp, represented a significant policy departure from the past. It stated that under certain circumstances, it would be in the national interest:
- to licence the export of large blocks of firm power to United States utilities to permit the development of large scale remote hydro or other power projects which would not be viable unless supported by the export for long periods of a significant proportion of the power generated.
In spite of this change, which allowed facilities to be built mainly for export, the regulation of electricity exports at the federal level remained important in Canada for a number of reasons. Indeed, there have historically been several reasons for the close regulation of electricity production and sale internationally and between the provinces at the federal level.
These are political and economical reasons. They include, for example, ensuring the security of supply for Canadian consumers and ensuring quality of access regardless of the region in which one lives.
The official opposition critic mentioned earlier the case of Prince Edward Island which has no electric generating capacity itself but relies on imports from other provinces.
A third reason is to assist in regional development. As well, there is the question of balancing interests of investors with over-all public interest. These interests
National Energy Board
may from time to time diverge. They may in fact compete.
For example, electric monopolies are shielded from competition and can raise prices well above the cost of supply. They can engage in price discrimination between customers. They can prevent competition for export markets by denying access to transmission systems. An electrical generation project may be profitable from the perspective of investors but may be undesirable from a national perspective once all of the associated costs, such as the flooding of huge areas of land, are factored in. A project may be desirable from a provincial perspective but not from the perspective of other provinces.
For example, if a province chooses to generate large amounts of electricity through the construction of a very large coal fired generating plant, that can result in airborne pollutants being carried away to a neighbouring province.
Of course short-term perspective may cause future generations to pay higher prices than would otherwise be the case. For example, the exploitation of our most favourable, most easily accessed, most easily developed hydro sites now for export, leaving distant, costly sites for future development for domestic use later.
All these concerns are legitimate. All should be addressed by any responsible federal Government. None should the take the back seat to short-term political or economic considerations or to facile ideological arguments. This is especially important given the critical nature of electricity in Canada's economy and energy future.
It has been argued by some that electricity is a commodity like any other; that like oil and natural gas it should be deregulated; that it is a value added product, indeed a manufactured good in essence; and that it should be deregulated as the oil industry was in 1985 and as the national gas industry was in 1986.
Surely we can agree in this House that electrical energy is not a commodity like any other. The NEB has recognized this in its report on the regulation of electricity exports released in 1987, where it noted:
An essential commodity might be defined, as one on which a country's security, economic health or the well-being of its population depends heavily and for which there are no close substitutes readily available at reasonable cost. The Panel believes that electricity qualifies as an essential commodity in most uses.

National Energy Board
Over time, alternative energy forms could replace electricity in some applications; however, in most applications, there are no reasonable substitutes for electricity, even over the long term.
Even the previous Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, the Minister of Communications (Mr. Masse), took great pains to emphasize the importance of electricity in his speech on November 26, 1987 to the Board of Directors of the Canadian Electrical Association, wherein he said:
Electricity's importance cannot be overestimated. It is essential to our civilization. Without it, we would not be lighting our buildings by merely flicking a switch. Our advanced medical treatment systems would not exist. There would be no radios, no television, no computers.
All the more important, one might add, to have a policy that will protect the interests of Canadians now and into the distant future.
The existing system of electrical export regulation has been clearly outlined in a background paper issued by the Minister of Communications last September. It is the system which has been in operation for many years now and has served Canada well thus far. It features, in summary, the following elements: the board issues export licences and orders for periods not exceeding 25 years; the board authorizes the construction and operation of international power lines, which are lines connecting a place in Canada to a place in the United States; in cases designated by the Governor in Council, the board regulates interprovincial power lines, which are lines from a place in a province to a place in Canada outside that province; and the board regulates the detailed routing of international and designated interprovincial power lines.
The procedure for exports and the procedure for power lines are essentially the same under the current legislative and regulatory regime. Except in very minor cases, the board conducts a public hearing and has regard to all relevant considerations. If the board finds that the proposal is in the Canadian public interest, it recommends to the Governor in Council that it be approved. Otherwise, the board denies the relevant authorization.
With respect to exports, there are two criteria which the board now focuses on: first, whether the export is surplus to reasonably foreseeable Canadian requirements and, second, whether the export price is just and reasonable.
With respect to power lines, the board focuses on the economic and technical viability of the line, on socioeconomic considerations and on the environmental impacts associated with the proposed route.
In addition to assessing applications with respect to the above criteria, the board also ensures that proposals adhere to relevant environmental standards and that export authorizations do not exceed 25 years in duration.
This regulatory regime will be changed by Bill C-23 in four principal aspects. First, and in many cases the most important, the provincial jurisdiction will now be the jurisdiction at which the advisability of export applications is determined. It will now be at the provincial level where the questions surrounding the proposed export are dealt with and some kind of recommendation devised.
Second, on the basis of this provincial work, the National Energy Board will routinely grant export permits in most cases. It is expected that in only a few cases will licences in the case of electricity exports or certificates in the case of power lines, both of which would occasion public hearings, be required. So long as the sponsoring province has complied with relevant federal environmental processes and so long as provincial regulations are deemed to be sufficient, exporters need only obtain a permit and can thereby usually avoid a federal public hearing.
Third, the maximum duration of export licences and permits will be increased from 25 years to 30 years.
Fourth, the National Energy Board will be required to begin to recover its costs.
How will these changes affect electricity trade over the decades? It is difficult to make firm predictions, but a number of concerns must be addressed. Let me elaborate.
First, public hearings for export applications will be rare because of what will now be the usually routine granting of permits. There is no compelling reason for making public hearings less frequent, especially given the importance of electricity to our national energy future. There has been no good evidence presented to the effect that the public hearing process has been overly burdensome in the past. Real duplication in the public hearing process is likely a rather rare thing and certainly not routine between federal and provincial agencies involved. Public hearings address issues of national
June 26, 1989

importance as distinct from items of provincial importance.
It is very difficult to anticipate all aspects of national interest based upon review from the provincial perspective. For example, it is conceivable that a utility or a provincial Government and its neighbour would both be in favour of a given export proposal, even though it may not be in the national interest in the long term. The NEB would be placed in the difficult situation of trying to anticipate these national interests without a national hearing. In fact, some provinces have review processes that can only be considered rudimentary.
A closed process seldom serves the public purposes well. It is not surprising that some utilities find the current process inconvenient, troublesome, even vexatious at times, although it should be remembered that the NEB has never refused an export application. Granted it has forced some alterations in applications, but it has never refused one.
It is possible under the new regime that the occasional export contract might be held up, even lost, but in our democratic system there is no good substitute for open public fora to protect the public interest. The process proposed in Bill C-23 forces the NEB to address the concerns of the public in a way that is not open, in a way that is inadequate, and in a way in which the criteria of the people of the country cannot reasonably be represented. The process that we now have forces the NEB to address the concerns of the public in the open using criteria that are clear and obvious to everyone.
Second, the Bill could politicize the making of decisions regarding whether to grant simply a permit or hold public hearings. Under the proposed system, the NEB would recommend to Cabinet that a public hearing be held if there is any reason to believe that the proposal may not be in the public interest. So far so good. However, the final decision on this is made by the Cabinet, not the NEB. This means that a decision made under this system is much more likely to be made on political grounds, and this could threaten regional interests. For example, a small province with few votes and few seats in Parliament could suffer if the Cabinet
National Energy Board
backed the export application of a more powerful neighbouring province for political reasons.
This could threaten the national interest. For example, Cabinet could side with an exporting province regardless of the national interest, if Cabinet saw that it was politically advantageous for some reason or other to do so.
This could certainly threaten the NEB. For example, if Cabinet reverses an NEB recommendation, vis-a-vis an important export proposal, if but once the NEB recommends to Cabinet that on a particular proposal public hearings must be held, and Cabinet says "no", the likelihood of Cabinet not accepting a given recommendation in future would likely figure prominently in the NEB's deliberations.
In other words, it would hobble the NEB as an effective regulatory body. Once overruled by Cabinet, the credibility of the NEB would be shattered and its future considerations would always have to be taken under the cloud of that disapproval. This would spell the end of the NEB authority as we know it.
Third, the maximum duration of export licences and permits will increase under these amendments from 25 years to 30 years. There has been no good justification for this increased alienation of a valuable Canadian resource. Until one is provided, the current duration of 25 years should remain.
I would like to note that those who are familiar with the speeches of the Hon. Minister of Communications, as I am becoming increasingly, will have noted his fondness for commencing each speech with a quote from some famous authority or person of letters. I will spare everyone here the detailed experience, but he began his speech of November 26, 1987 by outlining the proposed policy changes with a quote from Montesquieu as follows:
No alteration should be made in a law without sufficient reason.
No sufficient reason has been given in this case for the increase from 25 years to 30 years of the maximum duration of export licences and permits. I challenge the Government to provide one or to withdraw this part of the amending legislation.
Fourth, the National Energy Board under this Bill will be forced to recover its costs. Presumably this means

June 26, 1989
National Energy Board
from the utilities requesting export permits or licences. This will likely mean higher electricity rates for consumers in Canada, which is another form of regressive taxation.
Fifth, the Government's strategy of making electricity exports easier is all the more worrisome, given the proportionality clause in the Free Trade Agreement. Reducing public hearing processes to increase exports would be bad enough in itself, but this is made more serious by the fact that electricity exports come under the proportionality clause of the FTA. In times of energy emergency, we will be forced to export the same proportion that we exported from Canada for the previous three years. Meanwhile the Government is keen to increase this proportion by reducing the review process here in Canada.
Sixth, making exports easier also runs the risk of Canadians paying higher, not lower, prices for electricity in the future. As Tanis Mathers, of the Consumer's Association of Canada put it, as reported in The Montreal Gazette for September 8, 1988:
Canadians could could wind up paying higher prices because utilities could lock themselves into long-term contracts, making future electricity supplies scarce for domestic consumers.
He said directly, and I quote:
The fear is that-new projects needed to fill the demand at that time may be more expensive and increase electricity rates for domestic consumers.
This view is echoed by the NEB in its report on the regulation of electricity exports from 1987, where the board noted:
Unlike many manufactured products, most Canadian electricity production may be subject to increasing costs. Utilities generally develop their more favourable hydro sites first. Thus, if any but the costliest sites were developed to service the export market, the selling utility would have to develop a more expensive hydro site to service Canadian demand earlier than without exports. This means that, because of exports, Canadians would pay more sooner for their electricity. Similarly, nuclear safety and siting is expected to become increasingly costly over time, so that more rapid development in the short-run may mean higher prices for Canadians sooner than otherwise.
Those are the major concerns with the Bill as presented to us. Those are the concerns that we will be addressing in committee.
There are other questions as well. I think the principal question that the Government has yet to answer is: Why
are we doing this? Why are we changing the statutory and regulatory regime governing the export of electricity from Canada to the United States, and why are we doing it at this time? There are those uncharitable souls among us who would offer the perhaps jaundiced view that this indeed is a pay-off to Mr. Bourassa, the Premier of Quebec, in return for that individual's-let us be kind-tacit support for the current Government at the last federal election. It can be noted that the Bourassa Government of Quebec maintains no independent regulatory agency of hydro production, transmission and export in that process, leaving just Quebec Hydro and the Quebec Government as the regulators of future exports sales from that province to the U.S.A.
Just recently we saw a massive new sale of Quebec Hydro power to the United States at a time when most industry forecasters are saying that Ontario is facing increased electricity needs over the next while which could necessarily occasion the construction of new, large and perhaps numerous nuclear plants in Ontario. This is at the same time as cheap Quebec Hydro power is going to the United States. Question No. 1 is why are we doing this at this time?
Question No. 2 is of much greater detail, if Hon. Members will bear with me.
What status is the current first price guideline in this Bill? Under the National Energy Board Part VI regulations, subsection 6(2)(z)(i), an applicant is required to demonstrate that the export price "would recover its appropriate share of the costs incurred in Canada". This ensures that all costs, including the indirect costs that are difficult to quantify, that Canada incurs as a country but which are not borne by the exporting utility are taken into account in the export price. How are these costs, including extra-provincial impacts of a facility, for example, to be quantified and addressed under the provisions of this Bill? We do not know.
Finally, there are some miscellaneous considerations that the House may wish to entertain as it continues to consider this Bill. Because of the provisions of the Free Trade Agreement with the United States which require we sell to the United States under conditions identical to those under which we sell in Canada, it is virtually impossible for Canada to spur economic diversification and regional development using the natural advantage of
June 26, 1989

the plentiful electrical power we can generate in Canada.
As well, the emphasis of this Bill is toward supplying an ever greater amount of electricity to the United States, toward supplying or attempting to supply an apparently insatiable demand. Supplying this demand obviously brings with it benefit for Canada in terms of jobs and economic activity. It also brings environmental and other problems.
It needs always to t>e remembered that curbing demand can create jobs as well, and it is this focus that will lead us toward a more sustainable future. Random examples of this are light bulbs that use less electricity or producing electrical appliances for export that use much less power.
We must think of acid rain, nuclear waste, flooding valleys and the greenhouse effect when we think of electricity exports. In this context, electricity will be seen to be ever more strategic in nature. Natural gas, alternative fuels and hydroelectric power will be seen to be clean by more and more people and will be more valuable and in demand in the future. It will be more essential to the maintenance of a clean, environmentally healthy nation.
The Government, unfortunately, appears to want to alienate a greater share of one of our most valuable, most strategic natural resources, our electrical power. It is indeed ironic to reflect on the speech made by the Hon. Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Epp) to the B.C. Hydro's second annual energy forum held on May 11, 1989, when he said:
To ensure that we continue to have one of the world's highest living standards, we will need to increase dramatically the amount of electricity we generate-over the next 25 to 30 years, Canada will probably have to double its present electrical generating capacity.
This is from a Minister who is overseeing a Bill through this Parliament that will make greatly easier the export of our hydroelectrical power or electrical power generated through other means to the United States.
There are too many problems in this Bill. There are too many questions it leaves unanswered. Until those problems are addressed and until those questions are answered, we cannot support this Bill.
National Energy Board

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean J. Charest (Minister of State (Youth) and Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur State) and Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Youth), Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) and Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Minister of State (Youth); Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: NATIONAL ENERGY BOARD ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened to my two colleagues, the critic of the Liberal Party of Canada the and Member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys (Mr. Ma-cLellan) and the Member for Edmonton East (Mr. Harvey), who have presented, I presume, their party's position on Bill C-23. You will not be surprised if I tell you straight off that the Government does not share the opinions of my colleagues from the opposition parties. I am sure the public will not be surprised to hear this either, except that there are some arguments which, I think, should be voiced with great caution.
I am thinking, in particular, of the argument put forward a few minutes ago by my colleague from Edmonton East (Mr. Harvey) which is in fact an argument we frequently hear when a bill presented in the House of Commons does not please everyone; obviously, it must be Quebec's fault, this must be a favour to Robert Bourassa. That is not a very original argument, Mr. Speaker. It lacks depth and I would even say it is somewhat lacking in good will, especially this week as we will soon be celebrating our country's anniversary. Anyway, that is not the kind of argument I will use put forward to introduce Bill C-23.

The purpose of the Bill is twofold. First, it gives effect to the Government's policy respecting the regulation of electricity trade announced in September of 1988. Second, it provides for a number of minor changes in the National Energy Board Act that will reduce costs to the Government and will clarify the responsibilities of the board.
The critic for the Liberal Party and the Hon. Member for Edmonton East (Mr. Harvey) mentioned that this legislation was first enacted in 1959. By virtue of its age, I think we could easily draw the conclusion that legislation enacted in 1959 and revisited in 1989 would normally require modernization to make it more responsive to the needs and energy problems of the 1990s leading up to the new century. It is quite obvious that this legislation needs to be revisited since it deals with a sector in which activity is so intense and the pace of change is so rapid.

June 26, 1989
National Energy Board
The National Energy Board's present regulatory responsibilities with respect to electricity may be briefly summarized as follows: First, the board issues export licences and orders for periods not exceeding 25 years. Second, the board authorizes the construction and operation of international power lines. Third, in cases designated by the Governor in Council, the board regulates intraprovincial power lines. Finally, the board regulates the detailed routing of international and designated interprovincial power lines.
In describing how the system of regulating works, it is useful to distinguish the board's procedures from the board's review criteria. The procedures for reviewing export applications and the procedures for reviewing power line applications are essentially the same. Except in very minor cases, the board conductsa public hearing and has regard to all relevant considerations. If the board finds that the proposal is in the Canadian public interest, it recommends to the Governor in Council that it be approved. Otherwise the board denies the relevant authorization.
With respect to exports, there are two principal criteria that the board now applies. The first is whether the export is surplus to reasonably foreseeable Canadian requirements and the second is whether the export price is just and reasonable.
With respect to power lines, the board focuses on the economic and technical viability of the lines, on socioeconomic considerations and on the environmental impacts associated with the proposed route.
There are two main reasons that this Act needs to be changed. The first is that the regulatory procedures now in place are capable of improvement in several important ways. Second, the criteria the board applies in assessing applications are no longer as pertinent as they were when the Act was introduced in 1959.
The problem with the existing procedures is that they result in an unwarranted duplication of provincial regulation. In 1959, most provinces did not have mechanisms in place to regulate electricity exports. Today, all exporting provinces regulate their exports in one way or another. This means that federal regulations should focus on complementing rather than duplicating what the provinces already do.
The problem with the criteria that the board applies in assessing applications for electricity exports and international power lines, is that it does not adequately reflect today's realities. I can give two examples of what I mean.
In 1959 when the National Energy Board Act was introduced, most provinces did not regard themselves as exporters, and several anticipated that they might become electricity importers. Flence, there was a need for the National Energy Board to pay particular attention to whether a proposed export would be surplus to Canadian requirements. Today, all provinces are self-sufficient in generating capacity, and nine provinces regard themselves as electricity exporters or potential exporters.
My friend, the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys (Mr. MacLellan) of the Liberal Party referred to Prince Edward Island a few times during his remarks, quite justifiably so, and I would tend to guess that the only province that would not consider itself to be a potential exporter of electricity would be the Province of Prince Edward Island. However, today, all other provinces, contrary to 1959-and that is the difference-consider themselves, if they are not already exporters, as potential exporters of electricity. That has been a great change since the Bill was first brought in.
This does not mean that surplus considerations are now irrelevant. Quite the contrary. However, it does mean that it no longer needs to be one of the two or three dominant factors determining whether or not an export application is in the Canadian interest.
A second example, and perhaps the most important one, concerns the environment. The existing Act does not mention the environment in the key section that lists the considerations that are to be examined by the board in its determination of whether a proposed export is in the public interest. This is unsatisfactory in light of what we know today about the importance of environmental protection. In this context, it is evident that a new approach to electricity regulation is required.
I would now like to identify the fundamental principle upon which the new system of regulation is to be based. The essence of our federal system of Government is the distribution of powers between a central legislature and distinct provincial legislatures such that each is autonomous within its own sphere of jurisdiction. Unfortunately, the practice of federalism is often not a very easy one, as the Hon. Member for Edmonton East knows very well. Spheres of jurisdiction sometimes overlap, and this tends to lead to a duplication by two levels of Govern-
June 26, 1989

ment. Such duplication, where it is unwarranted, is a burden that the public should not have to support.
Under the Canadian Constitution, the provinces have jurisdiction over electricity generation, except for nuclear power, and intraprovincial power lines. The Government of Canada has jurisdiction over electricity exports, international power lines, and interprovincial power lines. Jurisdiction over interprovincial electricity trade is shared by both levels of Government.
However, because of the manner in which the Canadian electrical industry has evolved, those matters formerly within the Government of Canada's jurisdiction, tend to be extensively governed by provincial policies and laws. It is the provinces that decide whether electricity will be produced for export. It is not the federal Government, but the provinces. It is the provinces that decide the extent to which their utilities will engage in interprovincial trade. It is the provinces that govern the management of the provincial electrical grids. It is provincially-owned or provincially-regulated entities that initiate and conclude electricity trade transactions.
These facts suggest that the Government of Canada should design a system for regulating electricity exports that will function by exception. Where provincial regulation is sufficient to protect the Canadian public interest, federal regulation is not warranted; where provincial regulation is insufficient, the federal Government must have the full authority to act. In other words, the National Energy Board should complement and not duplicate measures taken by provincial Governments. This is the basic principle underlying the amendments contained in this Bill.
I now wish to describe the new regulatory procedures set forth in this Bill as they apply to the regulation of electricity exports and international power lines. The regulation of interprovincial power lines, which I shall come to later, will be different in certain important respects.
National Energy Board
Applicants for an export authorization or authorization to build an international power line will continue to submit their proposals to the board. Upon receiving the application, the board will ensure that notice is published in The Canada Gazette, and in such other media as are likely to be seen or heard by interested parties. The board will then carry out an initial screening of the applications. If the board is satisfied that the assessments carried out by the sponsoring provinces have adequately addressed all relevant concerns, the applicant will receive Canadian government authorization in the form of a National Energy Board permit.
A permit will not require a public hearing, nor will it require Governor in Council approval. However, and this is the important point to make, if there is a need to complement the measures carried out by the sponsoring provinces, then the board will recommend to the Governor in Council that a public hearing be carried out. Thus, the full authority of the federal Government will remain. It may be of some comfort to Members of the House and the public to know that the board's advice will also be made public.
If the Governor in Council accepts the board's recommendation, there will be a public hearing. Any such hearing will be conducted by the National Energy Board, and the board will have regard to all relevant considerations. Once the hearing is completed, the board will either deny the application or else recommend that a licence, in the case of exports, or a certificate in the case of power lines, be issued. Certificates and licences will not be issued until they have been approved by the Governor in Council.
In addition to those changes regarding the procedure for the authorization of exports and power lines, there will also be changes in the way that the detailed routing of international power lines is determined. The National Energy Board will, in all cases, authorize the general corridor through which the line will pass. The precise location of the line within this corridor will then be determined by provincial regulatory procedures and any expropriation that may be necessary will also be carried out under provincial laws.
The only exceptions to this general procedure will be in cases where the applicant elects to have federal law govern precise location and construction of an international power line. Upon such an election, the line will automatically be designated for a certification proceed-

June 26, 1989
National Energy Board
ing. Applicants seeking to build power lines will therefore always have the choice of whether provincial or federal law will govern detailed routing and land acquisition. It is anticipated that most will choose provincial law in order to avoid regulatory duplication. However, there may be instances where the applicant would prefer that federal law applied. This could happen, for example, where a line is opposed by one of the provinces through which it is to pass. That is consistent with the role that a federal Government would want to play in the area of energy: to be there and to be able to intervene as an arbiter in such cases where from time to time there are difficulties between provinces. We know that at any time there may be those types of difficulties, but the Act does enable us to intervene in such a case.
It is proper that the National Energy Board should conduct a public hearing to determine whether construction of the line should be authorized. The board should also have the power to ensure that the line, once authorized, can in fact be built. The board's powers regarding the detailed routing will thus be retained for just this purpose.
The procedures for the regulation of interprovincial power lines are unchanged from those set forth in the present National Energy Board Act. For the most part, such lines will be regulated by the provinces through which they pass. However, the Governor in Council may make orders designating that the line be certificated by the National Energy Board. When such an order is made, the detailed location and construction of the line will be governed under federal law.
I have already mentioned to you, Mr. Speaker, the basic principle governing the new policies that there should be no unwarranted duplication of federal and provincial regulations. It follows that the National Energy Board should concentrate on those aspects of a proposal that may not have been sufficiently dealt with by provincial regulatory procedures. The Bill states that in deciding whether there is a need to complement measures carried out by the provinces the board shall have regard to all considerations that appear to it to be relevant. This means that the board's purview will not be limited in any way. That is a very important point for this House. However, in order to give some guidance to
applicants, the Bill does cite three specific criteria not limited in any way that we will want the board to look at.
To begin with, the board will consider any impacts that a proposed export or international power line might have outside the sponsoring provinces. The second criterion will be the environmental impacts of the proposal and in particular whether it complies with federal environment standards. Finally, the board will consider whether Canadians wishing to buy electricity to serve their own domestic needs have been able to do so on terms no less favourable than the terms being offered to export customers. Thus I think the Hon. Member from Edmonton will be happy to know that the words of the Right Hon. John Diefenbaker which he cited would still find some effect in today's legislation. I can only assume that the Hon. Member from Edmonton would be happy that the policy put forward by the Conservative Government at that time is still respected, something for which he wished in his speech.

Mr. Speaker, my colleague from Edmonton East has also mentioned his concerns regarding the fact that under this legislation we could authorize the period of export, that we could issue periods of more than 25 to 30 years.
And the Member for Edmonton East argues that he does not know, that he has no idea why- Well, it's really quite easy to understand! The reason, Mr. Speaker, is to enable us to undertake large projects, hydro-electricity projects requiring massive investments, several billion dollars worth of investments. And there is no great mystery in that, you don't have to look very far, you only have to look at the energy sector, the oil sector, which also require considerable investments. If you're going to drill in the ocean, that requires considerable investments. Those investments have to be financed.
Mr. Speaker, we in Quebec know a thing or two in this area, thanks to Hydro-Quebec. We have financed several mega-projects in the last several years and it takes a certain time to amortize the costs and reimburse the loans. It's as simple as that, that's not so difficult to understand, except we thought that a 25-year period might be a bit tight and, without necessarily coming up with the perfect measure, because the financial markets also change a lot, we said to ourselves: We'll extend it to 30 years, that will give us extra leeway and enable us to better finance the mega-projects we are considering throughout Canada. Some of these projects will be developed in Quebec, unfortunately for the Member for
June 26, 1989

Edmonton East who does not like Quebec nor Mr. Bourassa very much, but other projects are planned for other regions of Canada, namely in British Columbia and in Alberta. We want to be able to take advantage of this natural resource everywhere in the country.
So, that is why we have decided that the permits should be valid for 30 years instead of 25. There's nothing very complicated in that!

I would now like to summarize the amendments that do not relate specifically to electricity. These are being introduced to reduce costs, to streamline the board's operations, to reflect the reduced level of regulation that has resulted from a more market-based approach to energy policy and to make other minor improvements to the Act. I was hoping there would not be a great clamour when I used the words "more market-based approached". It looks as though members of the Opposition were able to resist commenting on those words.
First, the number of board members is being reduced from 11 to a maximum of nine. The associate vice-chairman positions are to be eliminated.
Second, the board is to be given cost-recovery powers consistent with our over-all approach to deficit reduction announced in the Budget.
Third, the powers of the board with respect to such matters as accident inquiries, accounting practices and repairs are to be clarified.
Finally, a number of other minor changes such as the redefinition of certain terms are introduced to facilitate the application of the Act.
This Bill demonstrates that despite what the critics of the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement have been saying, Canada's energy interests are still fully protected. Electricity exporters must continue to obtain authorization from the National Energy Board. The amendments state quite explicitly that an application may be denied if it has unacceptable extraprovincial effects, if it has significant adverse environmental impacts and if Canadians wishing to buy electricity have been denied fair access to the electricity. The Bill thus proves that the
National Energy Board
Free Trade Agreement does not undermine the National Energy Board's ability to protect Canadian interests.
The Bill also demonstrates that the federal Government will not compromise its responsibilities with respect to international or interprovincial trade. All international power lines and all electricity exports will continue to require National Energy Board authorization. The Governor in Council will retain the power to designate interprovincial power lines as lines requiring a National Energy Board certificate.
As regards the detailed routing of power lines, the amended National Energy Board Act will state that while in most cases the relevant procedure will be provincial, applicants can, if they so wish, elect to have federal procedures apply. The Bill asserts that the federal Government will continue to exercise its authority to protect Canadian energy interests.
The amendments contained in the Bill will also provide a powerful incentive for the provinces to develop more rigorous environmental protection procedures. Because new exports and international power lines account for only a very small portion of Canada's total electricity supply system, federal export regulation in the past has proven to be an ineffective way to ensure that adequate environmental standards and procedures are applied to new electricity projects. The federal objective is to ensure that all electricity projects, not just those few designed for export purposes, also obtain rigorous environmental scrutiny.
This Bill will give the provinces a strong incentive to apply such scrutiny by putting standards and procedures in place that are equivalent to federal requirements. The provinces will avoid having their export applications subjected to a second regulatory proceeding.
All of this sounds pretty logical to me. Maybe it is something a little foreign to the political process. However, I think this Bill stands out as a good example of the necessity for change in our society. This Bill would amend an Act enacted in 1959, which Act deals with an area of our national life that has been veiy turbulent. It has gone through a great many changes in a very short period of time. It has affected our national life. It has become part of our national culture. It is a piece of

June 26, 1989
legislation that needs to be updated and changed. It needs a new focus. That is what this Bill is about.
It is a piece of legislation that also reflects the way our country works and how it has evolved. In 1959, most provinces did not regulate electricity. Now they do. So is it necessary for the federal Government to also leap aboard and be there with them to over-regulate the regulators? Could we not play a role that is complementary one to the other? What this Bill is about is good Canadian common sense. We recommend it to this House very highly.
