subtopic: STATEMENTS PURSUANT TO S. 0.31
STATEMENTS PURSUANT TO S. 0.31
subsubtopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY THIRTHIETH ANNIVERSARY OF FOUNDATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today we celebrate the 30th anniversary of the opening of the St. Lawrence Seaway, a real triumph over geography.

From Thunder Bay to Sept Isles ships may travel freely through nine locks, canals, and channels, by climbing the equivalent of a 62-storey building.

The St. Lawrence Seaway remains one of the finest works of engineering in the world. The 20,000 workers who built it over a five-year period removed 210 million cubic yards of rock and earth.
The St. Lawrence Seaway has supported the economy of several regions of Quebec and Ontario for 30 years. We pay tribute to the workers who built it and to those who operate it today for their significant contribution to the Canadian economy.

subtopic: NORTHERN AFFAIRS
NORTHERN AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my constituents who reside in the Mackenzie Delta were interested to learn of the federal Government's probable assistance to the Governor of Illinois when he personally requested that the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Siddon) allow three whales to be exported from Hudson Bay to an aquarium in Chicago.
Northerners believe these projects should be justified on their economic and scientific merits and should not depend on a Minister's whim.
Residents of Aklavik in the Northwest Territories have been working on a different kind of whaling proposal, but when they asked for assistance from the same Minister, he advised them he would not help and that they should negotiate on their own with authorities in Alaska.
Similarly, other northerners have been requesting assistance from the Department of Indian and Northern Affairs for at least the last two years to acquire an export permit to remove some reindeer to points within Canada. They have not only received no permit from the federal Government, they have not even had the courtesy of a response.
We cannot all live in the States. At some point the Government is going to have to treat Canadians as well as it treats Americans.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: VIOLATION OF HUMAN RIGHTS IN CHINA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I, along with Alliance for Life and 26 other pro-life affiliated groups with over one million supporters, wish to express our utmost horror and dismay at the recent violent suppression of lives and human rights in China.
Equally important to this abhorrence is the coercion of Chinese mothers into killing their children by abortion. This involves the use of forced abortion and infanticide
June 26, 1989

against families that exceed their child quotas of more than one child.
The United Nation's fund for population activities has been promoting such activities in China and in other countries to the tune of millions of dollars every year. The United States, formerly one of the chief supporters of this program, has ceased its funding because of the coerced abortions in China.
Canada, however, continues to be a very generous contributor to this fund. I firmly believe that most Canadians want no part of it, either directly or indirectly.
I therefore call upon the Government to withdraw support of any or all such organizations which contribute to the destruction of unborn human beings by depriving them of their human rights.

subtopic: REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT
REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the latest annual report of the Construction Industry Development Council, submitted to the then Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion, made a number of recommendations.
The recommendation to contract out construction work to private industry will undoubtedly outrage workers across the country. The council reported:
Contracting out of construction work delivers known costs, timely completion, guaranteed performance, quality assurance and an increased tax base. This compares favourably to the unpredictable costs of construction work when public employees and equipment are used.
This theme of contracting out or privatizing is rapidly gaining momentum in the Canadian workplace. Recently, the aforementioned council, in conjunction with Industry, Science and Technology Canada, produced a pamphlet entitled Can you Afford not to Contract Out. Does this mean that the Government supports the recommendations of the council?

subtopic: TOBACCO PRODUCTS
TOBACCO PRODUCTS
subsubtopic: BAN ON SALE IN DRUG STORES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, recently the Canadian Medical Association released a statement which reads in part:
The (CMA) will encourage the public to buy prescription drugs and other health products from drug stores that do not sell tobacco products. In the opinion of the CMA, the selling of tobacco is incompatible with the primary purpose and role of the pharmacy. The pharmacist is a respected and trusted health care professional, not a seller of products that, when used precisely as intended by the manufacturer, cause disease and the premature death of over 35,000 Canadians a year.
I would like to commend pharmacies in the Kitchener area which do not sell or have stopped selling tobacco products. They include the Hoegler, Riepert, Queen South, Forest Hill, and Heritage Park pharmacies.
I would also like to encourage other drug stores in the Waterloo region and across Canada to follow their example by ceasing to sell tobacco products.

subtopic: FORESTS

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian L. Gardiner (Prince George-Bulkley Valley):
subtopic: FORESTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Forest Ministers from across Canada are meeting with the federal Minister today. Canadians are anxiously awaiting renewal of the six expired federal-provincial forestry agreements that have provided a significant contribution to reforesting our denuded forest lands.
The Minister has said previously that he would have signed agreements in place by this week and would release the bargaining position of the federal Government.
The Minister should live up to his word, the Government should live up to its word, and release the details of the new agreements and the bargaining position of the federal Government to Parliament. In short, failure to act now means that the future of our forests are threatened.

subtopic: S. O. 31 TRADE COMMONS DEBATES
INTERPROVINCIAL BARRIERS
INTERPROVINCIAL BARRIERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is time to break down the barriers to trade between our provinces. Canada's Constitution and the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade prohibit restrictions on the free movement of goods between provinces. Yet, in Canada today, our internal trading practices ignore our international obligations and defy our Constitution.
Barriers to trade between provinces reduce industrial efficiency, distort capital investment, adversely affect the international competitiveness of Canadian exports, inconvenience citizens, and strain national unity. Our national economy is Balkanized into ten smaller markets.
Provincial Governments have set up other less visible barriers to trade by imposing different labour standards, establishing procurement restrictions, and giving tax and industrial incentives to companies based within their borders.
The four western provinces have taken steps to alleviate this situation and have signed their own agreement to reduce trade barriers and provide open tendering for government purchasing. This is an excellent beginning.
It is ironic that while this country has negotiated an outstanding Free Trade Agreement with the United States, barriers to trade within our own country remain. In the last two years a joint federal-provincial committee has reached an agreement in principle on opening government procurement, but it requires the approval of the First Ministers.
There is no reason for further delay. We are strong enough to compete in the global market-place. We can surely compete at home.

subtopic: FINANCE
FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) assures the House that the new sales tax will not be a hidden tax and Canadians know about it, he should ask himself the following questions:
Does he know how much federal tax he paid the last time he filled his gas tank? Can he tell us what federal taxes apply to gasoline and what rates? Does he believe that 90 per cent of Canadians have any idea how much tax they pay at the gas pump? I expect not because the tax is built into the price of the product.
How will the Minister keep his promise that Canadians will know exactly what they are paying in federal sales
tax?
I have no doubt there will be a massive propaganda campaign undertaken by the Minister. No matter what that campaign costs, Canadians will still not know how much sales tax they are paying on their children's music lessons or dental bills. There is no doubt that we will see the expenditure of millions of dollars before an information blitz will be allowed to die a quiet death when the Government will then be free to increase and expand the tax behind the veil of secrecy.

subtopic: VAL D'OR REQUEST TO BE PART OF THE QUEBEC MAJOR JUNIOR HOCKEY LEAGUE
VAL D'OR REQUEST TO BE PART OF THE QUEBEC MAJOR JUNIOR HOCKEY LEAGUE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 29, 1976, the Municipality of Val d'Or applied for membership in the Quebec Major Junior Hockey League. On May 26, 1987, the Val d'Or drill operators took over this application. Abitibi-Temiscamingue has contributed 530 players to Quebec hockey at the junior, college, university and professional levels. Forty-four of these players went on to the National League, like Jacques Laperriere, Serge Savard, Rogatien Vachon, Pierre Larouche, Jacques Cossette, Rejean Houle, Robert Ritchie, the late Michel Briere, Eric Desjardins, Pierre and Sylvain Turgeon, to name only a few.
Some leaders of this major junior hockey league in Laval, Trois-Rivieres and Shawinigan seem to be afraid to face a team and an organization from Abitibi-Temiscamingue. Mr. Speaker, if the Val d'Or drill operators are refused a team for Val d'Or on August 11,1 suggest that the league change its name to the Quebec Monopoly Junior Hockey League (QMJHL).
June 26, 1989

subtopic: THE ENVIRONMENT
THE ENVIRONMENT
subsubtopic: VISIT OF U. S. SENATOR MITCHELL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canadians across this country were pleased to hear the news that the United States would bring in new laws to protect our mutual environment. This is certainly something that we are looking forward to. Parliamentarians in this House are delighted to see our American counterparts taking a genuine interest in our concerns over acid rain.
Tomorrow is especially remarkable since Canadians will welcome Senator George Mitchell, the majority House Leader in the U.S. Senate, to our capital. As a member of the Environment Committee, I look forward to his appearance at our committee hearing on Tuesday. We have in Senator Mitchell a politician who is not only determined to cleaning up the environment but, because of his position, he is also capable of making it a reality.
The Senator has long been deeply concerned with the preservation of a quality environment. He is well aware of the damages acid rain can inflict. His state, the State of Maine, has long been a target of S02 and NOx emissions. It is gratifying to see an ally in the driver's seat in the Senate.
I join all Canadians in wishing him every success in this important mission as he brings these proposals into law and as he visits Canada for two days where he will be making a major speech in Toronto on Wednesday.

subtopic: INDIAN AFFAIRS
INDIAN AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Native Arts Foundation was founded in 1985 by John Kim Bell, the first native North American symphony conductor.
The foundation provides scholarships to help native young people pursue studies in the arts. Since 1985, $250,000 in scholarships have been awarded to promising native students.
In October of this year, the foundation plans to take a successful ballet The Land of Spirits on national tour. This ballet showcases the richness of native Canadian cultures and deals with the devastating problems of alcohol. In addition to regular audiences, the foundation plans to provide special matinee showings to 18,000 native young people from reserves across Canada.
To date the foundation has raised $1.1 million from private sources and has sought support from the Secretary of State and from the Department of Communications for matching funds.
The proposal has been backed up by four cabinet Ministers by letter and by a former Minister of Indian Affairs.
I call upon the Secretary of State (Mr. Weiner) and the Minister of Communications (Mr. Masse) to act immediately so that matching funds will be made available to this project prior to the tour taking place in October.

subtopic: CANADA POST CORPORATION
CANADA POST CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canada Post Corporation recently announced its first profit in 30 years as a result of over charging Canadians and reducing services.
In my riding of York North door-to-door mail delivery in all new subdivisions, whether in Vaughan, Aurora, King City or Richmond Hill, have been replaced by supermailboxes. This policy seriously affects all residents in my riding and particularly the blind.
As a Member of the parliamentary Standing Committee on Human Rights and the Status of Disabled Persons, I cannot accept a corporate plan that does not provide boxes large enough for Braille transcripts or talking book material. The blind residents must cope with the dangers of heavy traffic at the supermailbox sites. I am requesting that the Government immediately guarantee home delivery for all blind, visually impaired, and other gifted Canadians.
The Government's obsession with profit making has created two classes of citizens: those who receive door-to-door delivery and those who collect their own mail.

June 26, 1989
Oral Questions
The Government must return to a corporate plan that once and for all places people first.

subtopic: POLLUTION
POLLUTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, newspaper reports over the weekend stated that a Canada-U.S. Government study shows that PCBs, Mi-rex, and 28 other hazardous chemicals are accumulating in higher and higher concentrations in the Niagara River as it flows from Lake Erie to Lake Ontario.
The study also shows that seven of the chemicals including PCBs and mercury are showing up at the river's mouth at Lake Ontario in concentrations exceeding government water quality standards.
This study is to be considered by officials from both countries at a meeting on Tbesday, in connection with the 1987 Protocol signed by the Governments of Ontario, New York, the United States, and Canada, which approved a 10-year plan to cut in half the volume of chemicals polluting the Niagara River.
This joint report serves to illustrate that the time for talk is over. The four Governments must now take steps to see that this problem is corrected as soon as possible, in order to protect the health of the people in southern Ontario and upper New York State.

subtopic: CANADA PENSION PLAN
CANADA PENSION PLAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like the House to take a moment to think about Jenny Swanson, a constituent. She is in her early sixties, unmarried, and formerly a waitress. Displaced by younger workers, she is on the Canada Pension's early retirement provision and receives a paltry $65 per month. Her friend, the same age, is married, has never worked, never contributed to Canada Pension Plan, but has a husband aged 65. As a result, she collects more than twice as much as Jenny does each month.
Surely it is time for the pension system in this country to be revised with a view to providing a liveable pension for the many, many Jennys in Canada who are trying to
exist on their Canada Pension Plan. Instead of talking about equality and fairness, the Government has to act.

subtopic: ABORTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the issue of abortion remains unsettled. When the Supreme Court struck down the previous law, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulro-ney) gave us in this Chamber the opportunity to vote freely on this very important matter.
Unfortunately, nothing was resolved by our vote on the motion and amendments presented to us at the time. Then the appeal of the Borowski case was dismissed by the Supreme Court on the grounds that it was moot. Their decision stated that:
The Court would, if it exercised its discretion, pre-empt a possible decision of Parliament, by dictating the form of legislation it should enact.

FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, until quite recently the Minister of Finance kept repeating that the present federal sales tax had three basic flaws, including the following one, which I quote from his folder, published under the title: Goods and Services Tax:
The current federal sales tax is hidden.
Mr. Speaker, my question for the Minister of Finance is this: Is it part of his Government's hidden agenda to use this hidden tax, which can be increased at any time, unilaterally and invisibly, in order to empty the pockets of Canadian taxpayers in the years to come?

subtopic: FINANCE
speechtext:
Absolutely not, Mr. Speaker. I think I have made it very clear that the existing tax is hidden. There is a 13.5 per cent rate and it is buried in the middle of the production process. The new goods arid services tax will be levied at the retail level at 9 per cent, and it will be very clear to Canadians what that tax rate is.
Let me remind the Hon. Member of the current effective federal tax rates at the retail level. For household appliances the lowest rate is 6.05 per cent and the highest rate is 12.67 per cent; for kitchen utensils the low rate is 3.82 per cent and the high is 10.72 per cent.
The point I am making is that currently the consumer cannot know what the tax burden is. Under the new system it will be very clear; it will be 9 per cent.

subtopic: VISIBILITY OF NATIONAL SALES TAX
VISIBILITY OF NATIONAL SALES TAX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, all the proposals for tax reform have called for a visible national sales tax. The only thing visible about the present position of the Minister of Finance is that because provinces refused to be coerced in April to accept a take it or leave it deal, the Minister decided to do the sneaky thing; in other words, do the deal and then hide it from everybody, all the time publishing pamphlets and insisting that it is going to be visible.
Will the Minister stand in his place today and demonstrate that he is capable of keeping his word and tell us unequivocally that the tax will be visible, that he will do what he said he was going to do as late as April 27 in his own pamphlet?

subtopic: VISIBILITY OF NATIONAL SALES TAX
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the 9 per cent tax rate will be quite clear. It will be 9 per cent on all taxable items for the consumer. Let me give another example to the Hon. Member. On office furniture today the low rate is 7.32 per cent and the high is 10.77 per cent. It is quite impossible for a consumer to know what the tax burden is today, but the tax burden under the new system will be 9 per cent.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR ADMINISTRATIVE REVIEW FOR REFUGEE CLAIMANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Employment and Immigration. This morning Members from both sides of the House heard very moving testimony from 50 refugee claimants living in Montreal. They came to Ottawa as representatives of the 125,000 people trapped in this huge backlog. Because of the prolonged delay in reviewing their cases, the claimants have been separated from their families and children, some for up to periods of four to five years.
Given that this is but one of the human dilemmas in this backlog, and given that a case by case review, which can take up to two or three years, is lengthy, expensive and a taxing review on the country, will the Minister consider a middle ground, an administrative review, so that families will not have to wait seven to 10 years to be reunited.

Mr. Speaker, I think it is important to point out that where the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees or a Canadian visa officer is of the opinion that an individual is in danger, measures can be taken to bring that person to Canada. However, as a general rule in processing the backlog cases, we intend to

June 26, 1989
Oral Questions
deal with the claimant in Canada before making any decisions concerning dependents abroad.
I would remind the Hon. Member that we have insured that those who are in Canada can work, which should help them in terms of supporting their families at home. We intend to move on the backlog as expeditiously as possible.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ACTION ON BACKLOG
REQUEST FOR ACTION ON BACKLOG
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that is what the Government said two or three years ago, move expeditiously. Now at the very best, that backlog processing will not start until probably the late summer or fall.
The Minister fully knows that these claimants have been in Canada for years, have established themselves in this country and formed the workforce backbone of many key sectors in Canada. I therefore ask the Minister, is it logical to spend taxpayers' dollars and go through the long exercise of removing and deporting these people when in fact levels may be increased next year and may possibly bring these people back? Is it not better to have an administrative review so that the Government and Ministers can say no to those who are clearly unworthy, and yes to those who are deserving and who are contributing to Canadian society?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration; Minister responsible for the Status of Women
subtopic: REQUEST FOR ACTION ON BACKLOG

It is very important that people who come here come under the same rules, whether they come in the refugee stream or they come in the immigration stream. This country welcomes people coming to Canada as genuine refugees and as immigrants but we expect them all to come under the rule of law.

subtopic: NON-SMOKERS' HEALTH ACT ALLEGED CONFLICT OF INTEREST
NON-SMOKERS' HEALTH ACT ALLEGED CONFLICT OF INTEREST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Deputy Prime Minister, better known as the former Prime Minister.
In light of information obtained under the Access to Information Act, Bill Neville, the Tory tobacco tout was given advance drafts of the regulations governing the Tobacco Products Control Act. This allowed him, through his lobbying efforts, to water down the health warnings to consumers in Canada while the health community did not become aware of the regulations until November, 1988. Can this Government justify one of its closest cronies, as a paid lobbyist of the tobacco industry, using his personal connections with the Government to influence their decisions? Is this not a clear case of conflict of interest?

speakeroldname: Hon. Perrin Beatty (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: NON-SMOKERS' HEALTH ACT ALLEGED CONFLICT OF INTEREST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if the facts were at all as the Hon. Member presents them, I would be very concerned myself. The facts are not however.
The Government has a very clear policy of sending out draft regulations for comment by the private sector, by industries which are affected and also by public interest groups which may have an interest in responding. An information letter was sent out on November 7 of last year. It was distributed widely, encouraging various groups to make presentations to the Government with regard to the draft regulations. Among the groups which did so was the Non-Smokers' Rights Association, whose brief dated November 16, 1988, dealt specifically with this.
If Mr. Neville was so effective in this case in influencing the Government's actions, perhaps the hon. gentleman could explain why tobacco taxes went up $4 a carton in the Minister of Finance's Budget earlier this year.

subtopic: BANK ACT

speechtext:
The House resumed from Monday, June 19, consideration of the motion of Mr. Loiselle that Bill C-9, an Act to amend the Bank Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, and the amendment of Mr. Rodriquez:
That the motion be amended by deleting all the words after the word "that" and substituting the following therefor:
"Bill C-9, an Act to amend the Bank Act, be not now read the second time but that it be read a second time this day six months hence".
Bank Act

subtopic: BANK ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak in opposition to Bill C-9, the amendments to the Bank Act. This Bill, with the exception of including small businesses in the Bill, is basically the same as Bill C-140 which died on the Order Paper with the last federal election.
I want to point out to the House that although I was not a Member of the debates and did not take part in those debates, my colleagues in the New Democratic Party opposed that Bill forcefully. Our opposition remains steadfast in light of this new piece of proposed legislation.
There are a number of reasons why we oppose this Bill. First, the Bill provides few guarantees for customers and small businesses against unfair service charges that have been applied by the banks. It does nothing to keep the fees and service charges under some degree of control.
We oppose the basic thrust and the basic principle of the Bill which is that the banks themselves can actually be trusted to keep service charges in line. The Bill is proposing that the banks police themselves. To a great extent, that is like asking the fox to guard the chicken coop.
The Government took the same position on interest charges on credit cards. Although the charges did come down initially when Parliament first put on the pressure, those charges have climbed right back up, if one cares to look at what has happened in the credit card industry. The concept of voluntary compliance or voluntary policing is a very weak concept. It has shown to be very ineffective.
I would like to point out some basic weaknesses in the Bill. With respect to voluntary compliance, the legislation does not force the banks to do anything about their service fees except to disclose the charges and to notify their customers about the increases and the new fees. In the case of small business, the banks are not required to disclose all their charges but only those that are defined in a core list.
I must say that the Government seems to be basing this approach on the assumption that the disclosure in the notification of charges will sort of open up the competition. However, I would like to point out that this really has very little impact in terms of a customer's ability to move from one bank to another. For example, if somebody has a mortgage or an outstanding loan and finds they have had a service charge applied to that item, it will be very costly for them to pull up stakes and move the business elsewhere. They are locked into the mort-

June 26, 1989
Bank Act
gage or the loan. They would just have to grin and bear it. There is very little latitude for the small business owner or for anyone who has a mortgage simply to pull up stakes without cost to themselves or to their business operations.
In that respect this Bill does very little in terms of opening up the concept of competitive rates between banks. The past record of the banks in terms of voluntary compliance has not been very good. The Royal Bank has a net income of over $700 million. The income of the Bank of Nova Scotia last year was some $506 million. The Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce had record earnings of $591 million. Despite these massive profits the banks did not hesitate to raise their service charges.
I will give an example of that, Mr. Speaker. The Royal Bank of Canada raised 15 of its service fees on November 1 from 4 per cent to 6 per cent. It raised the cost of writing an NSF cheque up to 12 per cent despite the fact that it had a banner year last year in terms of its profits. The Bank of Nova Scotia and the Imperial Bank of Commerce have also raised their service charges, again despite banner years in terms of the banking industry.
Those types of charges are tough on small businesses. I have spent quite a bit of time talking to small business owners in my constituency, the constituency of Okanagan-Shuswap. There are two major concerns that the owners and partners in small businesses have. The first is with respect to high interest rates. The second is with respect to the many hidden charges that are foisted upon small businesses. They are very concerned about the fact that the banking industry does not seem or appear to be the friend of the small business person. They do not appear to be there to help in making the small business sector flourish.
There is a lot of concern in my constituency, and probably in the constituency of eveiy Member of this House. The small business community is concerned about the high cost of borrowing money from the banks and of the high cost of simply doing business. As you will know, Mr. Speaker, just about every small business
across Canada is in some respect reliant on the banking community in order to operate.
In 1987 five major banks, the Scotia Bank, the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce, the Royal Bank, the Bank of Montreal and the Toronto-Dominion Bank, collected over $1 billion from bank service charges from the small business community, the investment community and people who have mortgages. That is a great deal of money. I would suggest that that level of profit-taking indicates that perhaps the service charges are too onerous and have to be brought down. In fact, they are unfair to the business community and to the taxpayer.
I wish to deal now with the charges that the Bill before us does not seek to remove. I refer to charges for deposits and withdrawals. To me, and I am sure to most Members, those are core services of a bank. One deposits money for safekeeping. When the time comes at which the money is needed, it is withdrawn. It is a core service. There should be no reason to apply service charges to this fundamental level of service that the bank is established to allow.
In terms of the service charge for cashing an NSF cheque, I remind the House that this charge was called offensive by the last Minister of Finance. Yet the banks, such as Toronto-Dominion, did not agree to comply voluntarily. It still charges customers for unknowingly cashing an NSF cheque. When a business cashes its cheques it has no idea which cheque will not be sufficiently funded. Yet that business is penalized by the bank for submitting such a cheque which in all innocence fails to be negotiable security.
The Bill does not protect the small business community from being charged. Quite frankly, in some areas of the country where the economy is marginal, some small businesses have a number of NSF cheques. Thus it becomes a burdensome charge on small business to have to pay a penalty for processing NSF cheques.
The legislation before us does not remove the charge for closing the account. This is also something we consider to be a core service charge of a bank. There are charges for going below a minimum balance and for providing the current balance of an account. If an individual or a company representative comes into a
June 26, 1989

bank and wants to find out what their current account level is, why should they be charged? That too is a core service.
Customers are being charged for errors made by the bank itself in the administration of an account. There is no reason that a service charge should be applied to that. The Bill does not prohibit any of these charges. It does not force the banks to provide a basic no-frills account which would provide these services free of charge.
The third point I would like to touch on is self-monitoring by the banks. One of the difficult aspects of this Bill-in fact it is a farce-is that the banks monitor themselves to see whether they have complied voluntarily in bringing their services into line. Again, it is a case of the fox being charged with guarding the chickens.
How can one expect the level of accuracy to be what it should be in terms of whether or not they have in fact complied? If customers are not happy with the way their complaints are dealt with, they should be allowed to contact the office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions in Ottawa. However, this is not a real guarantee because the Superintendent of Financial Institutions does not have a mandate to protect consumers. The Bill would only create more pressures for an agency which is already overworked and in fact is not established to do that kind of job. The Superintendent's job is to ensure that the banks stay in business, not that they satisfy consumers. In that respect, it is almost a conflict of interest.
Those are three critical areas of weakness in this legislation. Because of those weaknesses, I think the legislation should not see the light of day and in fact the Bill should be withdrawn.
We must accept the recommendations of the Finance Committee which has done a commendable task in uncovering many of the problems we are having with respect to the commercial banking industry. We should accept the recommendation to require the provision of a free basic, or core banking service which is, after all, the main reason why the banks were established originally.
Bank Act
We should accept the recommendation to prohibit certain unfair charges which I have already mentioned, including minimum bank balances and charge backs for cashing NSF cheques.
We agreed with these recommendations but we also feel they do not go far enough. We would like to propose additional recommendations to those made by the Finance Committee. There should be a freeze on all bank service charges for one year. Bank service charges have increased over the past five years at an annual rate of 19 per cent, far above the inflation rate. That is far above the necessary rate of increase in order to simply cover the increased cost of living. It is unjustifiable.
The banks generate about $1 billion a year from these service charges. Therefore a very strong argument can be made that the banks have overcharged Canadian consumers and the small business community in Canada. I believe they should be required to give Canadian businesses and consumers a fair break.
Also, we would recommend the establishment of a financial services ombudsperson who would be empowered to perform customary advocacy and referee services as well as to referee and develop long-term policy advice. I think it is an excellent suggestion in light of the fact that we have seen very strong evidence that the banks have been guilty of overcharging Canadian consumers.
In the last Parliament my colleague, the Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez), proposed legislation that would involve many of these recommendations by the Finance Committee as well as the proposal for a one-year freeze on bank charges and the concept of a financial services ombudsperson. The Bill would have extended these guarantees to all consumers and small businesses. Based on those recommendations, we would like to see this current legislation withdrawn. The appropriate amendments and valued criticisms that the Finance Committee has developed should be implemented into the legislation so that we can develop the kind of protective mechanisms for which the small business community has been asking and which the banks have been guilty of not providing.

subtopic: BANK ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when one listens to the Hon. Member from the New Democratic Party speak about the required changes to the Bank Act, it is amazing to realize that we have to raise in the House of Commons something that should have been regulated in law many years ago. If there is any legislation that should be rigid, it is the Bank Act.
For all practical purposes the banks have a form of monopoly that has been given to them by the Government. Yet year after year in the House we have to bring up the abuses by the banks in this country.
I have been a victim of service charges on many occasions. Recently I received four NSF cheques, each with a service charge of $15. Yet when one attempts to call the bank on which the money is drawn to see if there
is enough in the account, the bank will not give the information about whether the person has sufficient funds. It is necessary to go to one's own bank, get on one's knees and ask them to call the bank to see if there is sufficient funds before depositing the cheque. It is a catch-22 situation.
The rate at which service charges have been creeping up over the years is a disgrace. No matter what government is in power, it should immediately ensure that the Bank Act is the most rigid of all legislation because it deals with one of the most fundamental aspects of our democracy.
The core services provided by the banks operate on a very basic principle, the cost of doing business. If the banks cannot provide the service, why don't they get out of the business?

Mr. Speaker, I know that many of my fellow citizens have noticed that after going to the bank for whatever reason, their statement indicates a charge of $1, $1.50, $5 or $7. When you enquire, the bank says those are fees for this or that service, but these are fees that should not even exist.
And then we have to come here to argue this issue and say: This is abuse! Of course this is abuse, and if there ever was a place where such abuse should be stopped, that place is right here!
The Bill before the House today I must say am not familiar with the other attempts to legislate the matter in the past but I can inform the House that the Bill before it today is only an attempt to deal with the issue but at least we should respect the principle that any Canadian who receives a service from the bank-and don't forget that the bank gets its charter from the government so it is a kind of monopoly, and it gets very rigid.
No bank should have the right to decree unilaterally that it will charge fees for certain services. It doesn't make sense at all. And just the same, we have to come and argue this issue in the House.
Everybody deals in good faith. Of course there are exceptions. Why is it not understood that with our banking system, fundamentally small businesses have been complaining about the charges on NSF cheques and others? The fact remains that the banks should not
June 26, 1989

have the latitude to charge for any service to citizens of this country. This Bank Act is not rigid enough.
It is very simple. We have to get down and start from zero. The banks must be called to task and we must settle the problem once and for all. How many small business organizations, how many consumers have been heard on different news programs, on open-line radio programs telling us stories about creeping service charges that have increased through the years? Yet we cannot come up with an Act to right a wrong within what is a fundamental aspect of this country, our banking system.
I do not have to go into detail about banks' record profits, let alone the hundreds of millions of dollars in write-offs because of poor investments in Third World countries where it was thought the banks were going to make a mint. These proved to be failures. Yet they wrote them off, of course, against the taxpayers. It is an amazing coincidence that when the news was getting out that they were going to have to write off hundreds of millions of dollars of their loans to certain countries, all of a sudden the phenomena of the creeping charges came in. The charges escalated out of proportion.
It is very simple. I think we should put this Act aside, sit down again and take the recommendations from the committee on finance. We should call the banks to task and say: "You are not going to set the rules. We are going to set the rules when it comes to charges."
Basically our job is very simple. You can talk to any Canadian or to any small business organization and it is only common sense, they will tell you, that there should be no bank charges. That is obvious because it is their service and their cost of doing business.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Corbeil (Minister of Labour) moved
subtopic: NON-SMOKERS' HEALTH ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
that Bill C-27, an Act to amend the Non-Smokers' Health Act be now read a second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to explain to the House the proposed amendments to the Non-Smokers Health Act.
As you know, this legislation was the result of a Private Members' Bill introduced by Lynn McDonald, the former Member for Broadview-Greenwood. The health of Canadians is something that concerns us all, and you will recall that Bill C-204 received the support of Members on both sides of this House and of the Senate.
All Parties being agreed, Bill C-204 received royal assent in June 1988. Once again I want to congratulate the Bill's sponsor for her remarkable achievement in

Non-smokers' Health Act
difficult circumstances: obtaining Parliament approval of the concept of regulating the use of tobacco in the work place.
However, the legislation has not yet been promulgated because it contains a number of aspects that as difficult to administer and to enforce.
Being a Private Members' Bill, the legislation did not designate a specific minister who would be responsible for its implementation and enforcement. Pursuant to Order in Council of December 7, 1988, the Minister of Labour was made responsible for the Bill as it affected the work place, while enforcement on public carriers was assigned to the Minister of Transport.
Subsequently, Mr. Speaker, closer scrutiny of the legislative text by the two responsible departments together with Health and Welfare Canada revealed that in its present form, the legislation presented some enforcement problems. Personally, I think it is important to provide for an inspection mechanism and an enforcement process, both of which were lacking in the existing legislation. Obviously, when there are any doubts that its provisions will be observed, legislation loses its impact and effectiveness.
My concern for the practical aspects of enforcement led me to question the shortcomings in the current legislation and ask for permission to amend it. I would like to stress that the amendments being proposed today still observe the initial spirit and scope of the legislation adopted last year.
I firmly believe that these amendments which are intended to fill the gaps in the legislation and to make it easier to administer the Non-Smokers Health Act, will give the text more teeth and make it more effective. The amendments will not only correct a number of technical and drafting problems, they will also create an inspection and enforcement system that will make the legislation more meaningful.

The amendments provide for a system of inspection which will involve Labour Canada and Transport Canada inspectors and which they will carry out in addition to their ongoing duties. It is not anticipated that there will be any requirement for additional resources to undertake this work. Inspectors will carry out the provisions of the Act within the context of their ongoing inspections.
Indeed, I should point out that under the Act, employers have a responsibility to ensure that persons do not smoke except in designated smoking rooms or smoking areas. If an employee contravenes the Act, the employer would be expected after due warning to take disciplinary measures against that employee consistent with standard employer-employee disciplinary practices without recourse to the inspector. I believe this kind of infraction will prove to be the norm, and in large measure, the legislation will be self-regulating.

A parallel enforcement method is suggested, based on a system of fines, to complement the current mechanism. The system of fines was selected for the following reasons: It allows contravenors to plead guilty voluntarily, pay a fine and thus avoid summary proceedings; fines are used by other jurisdictions in Canada and abroad to enforce no smoking rules and also within the federal Government, more specifically by the Departments of Fisheries and Oceans and the Environment.
The Law Reform Commission of Canada recommends this approach to reduce the number of summary proceedings.
The fines will be similar to those applied in the case of traffic violations. Amounts will be determined by the regulations but will not exceed the limits stated in the legislation, which will remain unchanged.

There are also a number of drafting and technical problems with the Auditor General Act. These problems will be corrected through the amendments. For example, in the Act as it was passed, there is a requirement that the employer provide a smoke-free environment. The concept of a smoke-free environment implies a system of measurement. However, it is not technically or administratively feasible to measure concentrations of tobacco smoke to determine whether the environment is smoke-free or not. We need to have a practical and enforceable alternative that still retains the spirit and the intent of this original requirement. The amendments therefore will instead place a requirement on employers to ensure that persons refrain from smoking in the workplace except in designated smoking rooms or smoking areas.
June 26, 1989



Since it is easier to allow smoking in certain areas than to provide for a totally smoke-free environment, the concept will allow for more uniform and more effective implementation of this legislation.

However in the spirit of providing a smoke-free environment, designated smoking rooms in buildings, the construction of which commences after December 31, 1989, will need to be independently ventilated. Designated smoking rooms in older buildings will need to be independently ventilated to the extent reasonably practicable. Detailed technical requirements such as ventilation rates will be specified in regulations that will be developed in consultation with management and labour representatives.
Mr. Speaker, representatives of employers, employees and health groups support these amendments. I only hope that I can count on all Hon. Members of this House to support them just as much so that we can implement this Bill as soon as possible. The original Act was given Royal Assent nearly a year ago.
That is why I propose in clause 16 that the law take effect six months after the amendments receive Royal Assent, which I realize will give just enough time to put the necessary regulations in place.
This Bill is an important piece of non-partisan legislation which deserves to be applied effectively, in keeping with its original spirit and intent. It is a major step towards a healthier work environment for Canadians. I therefore count on the support of all Hon. Members of this House to pass this Bill.

subtopic: NON-SMOKERS' HEALTH ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to speak on this Bill although there was equal demand to be in my constituency where I was to hear the presentations of citizens respecting pension reforms.
The Liberal caucus supports the quick passage of Bill C-27. In fact, I would have given the Government an excellent rating for introducing Bill C-27 which proposes amendments to the Non-smokers' Health Act except
Non-smokers' Health Act
that in stalling for a year the Government almost killed the initiative of a private Members' Bill. The Non-smokers' Health Act, Bill C-204, sponsored by Lynn McDonald, was introduced and given first reading on October 6,1986, almost three years ago. The Bill was given Royal Assent on June 28, 1988, but was not proclaimed. Thus, the Non-smokers' Health Act has been in limbo for almost a year now.
This is not surprising given the Government's initial lack of enthusiasm for Bill C-204. When introduced, Lynn McDonald's private Members' Bill was apparently opposed by the federal Cabinet. However, opposition Members of Parliament teamed up with government back-bench Members of Parliament to force the passage of the Bill, a true example of non-partisan approach when it comes to the fundamental issue of health care and health safety.
Yet, after the Bill was given Royal Assent, the Government did not move quickly enough to proclaim it. Members from all Parties had to continually urge the Government to take action to proclaim the Bill or to introduce amendments to it. I myself, Mr. Speaker, urged the Government to make the Non-smokers' Health Act law when I delivered a statement under Standing Order 31 on the occasion of the beginning of the National Campaign for Action on Tobacco on May 16.
By neglecting the Non-smokers' Health Act for almost a year, the Government has illustrated its inability to translate the scientific evidence of a major epidemic into a corresponding appropriate political action and response. Moreover, the Government's reluctance to proclaim the Bill after it was given Royal Assent proved the Government's arrogant tendency to make a mockery sometimes of the decisions of Parliament. This delay also illustrated the Government's lack of concern for the health of Canadians when the lobby from tobacco industries became very strong.
As I have mentioned to the House before, Mr. Speaker, last year more than 35,000 Canadians died prematurely from diseases caused by tobacco. This total is greater than the total number of people who died as a result of accidents, suicides, homicides, AIDS, alcohol and alcohol-related totalities. Despite such statistics the Government postponed dealing with Bill C-204 for almost a year. In a sense this allowed continued health risks to occur.

June 26, 1989
Non-smokers' Health Act
The old cliche that it is better late than never does not quite hold true in this case. We expected more leadership on this vital issue from the Government. The Government's lengthy inactivity in regard to the Nonsmokers' Health Act causes us to question the credibility and ethics of the Government which does not seem to have the grace to respect the will of the House promptly.
By delaying action on this Bill, the Government allowed continued health risks to occur and thus set a poor example for the country. If justice is delayed, justice is denied. If a good cause is delayed, a good cause has been denied.
It is disturbing to realize that the Government cares so little about the welfare of Canadians that it would allow a good cause, restricting smoking in the workplace and therefore protecting the health and rights of non-smokers, to be denied for so long.
I am relieved to note that the Government has finally acknowledged its responsibilities and introduced Bill C-27 which proposes amendments to the Non-smokers' Health Act to provide for inspection and enforcement clauses which the original Bill, being a private Members' Bill, did not have the opportunity to include.
At this juncture I am delighted to laud the Government on the new structure of the Bill. Bill C-27 is organized so that the definitions are all at the beginning of the Bill, the enjoinders and the inspection clauses are in the middle, and the regulatory-making powers of the Governor in Council are at the end.
I would also like to congratulate the Government for removing Clause 3(6) from the original Bill which state: "Nothing in this Act affects any rights to protection from tobacco smoke at common law or under any Act of Parliament or of a provincial legislature". This provision would have allowed for the possibility of provincial variations in the application of the Non-smokers' Health Act.
Clause 6 of the new Bill states:
"Nothing in section 4 or 5 affects the operation of any other Act of Parliament or regulations thereunder or any rule of law in relation to the protection of persons from exposure to tobacco smoke.
This will ensure more consistent application in all the provinces.
The amendments made to Clause 5 are also to be commended. Whereas the original Bill included provisions for removal of smoking passengers from nonsmoking aircraft, the new Bill also includes provisions which extend this rule to buses and trains.
An additional positive feature of Bill C-27 is that under Clause 14, peace officers and persons employed to act as inspectors for the purposes of this Act may serve tickets to people who are smoking in non-smoking areas. This is important because there are certain workplaces where an employer does not have authority over all the people in the workplace. For example, it is difficult for a bank manager to order a customer to stop smoking. Now the customer will be deterred from smoking in nonsmoking workplaces by the risk of getting a ticket.
I would like to point out, however, that there is still a problem with the provision on ventilation, it is still a vague clause. Clause 3(4) of the original Bill stated: "Every employer shall make reasonable efforts to ensure that a designated smoking room is independently ventilated". The clause in the new Bill reads as follows:
"Where an employer has designated a room for smoking under subsection (2) in a building or portion of a building the construction of which commenced before January 1, 1990, the employer shall, to the extent reasonably practicable, ensure that the room conforms to any requirements of the regulations respecting independent ventilation of designated smoking rooms."
Now an employer can argue not only that efforts to provide ventilation would be unreasonable, but that they would be impracticable as well. We should ensure that this does not happen.
The new Bill also results in a time delay for when rooms designated as smoking rooms have to be independently ventilated in newly constructed buildings.
The old Bill required buildings constructed prior to January 1, 1990 to have ventilation in smoking rooms only if this could be done with reasonable effort. The new Bill allows the reasonably practicable clause to apply to all buildings, the construction of which began before January 1, 1990, regardless of when construction is finished.
In addition, in the new Bill the requirement for independent ventilation is removed from the legislation and put into the regulations. I urge the Department,
June 26, 1989

June 26, 1989
Non-smokers' Health Act
Researchers are now discovering that nicotine changes the very structure and function of the brain. I quote now from the U.S. Congressional Quarterly editorial research report of March 24, 1989: "Nicotine controls the release of hormones from the pituitary gland in the brain and from the adrenal gland in the body. It stimulates adrenalin, which may produce the same symptoms as physical and psychological stress. Nicotine also stimulates the release of dopamine and noradrenalin, which may produce feelings of pleasure. Autopsies have found that heavy smokers develop additional nicotine receptors, sites on the surface of brain cells that provide entry points for nicotine.
These changes in the brain, if permanent, might explain why some smokers say they never regain their abilities of mental concentration years after quitting. Another possibility is that such smokers are suffering some form of long term withdrawal.
What is also important to note is that the earlier one starts smoking, the longer one will smoke. Thus it is important to stop smoking before it starts with the young people.
According to a survey conducted by the U.S. National Institute on Drug Abuse, over 25 per cent of the high school seniors who ever smoked had their first cigarette by Grade 6, over 57 per cent had their first cigarette by Grade 8 and 94 per cent had their first cigarette by Grade 11.
According to the same survey, the highest rates of initiation into daily smoking are among children who are 12 to 14 years of age.
Cigarette smoking is the future No. 1 killer of today's teenagers. According to an article in The Journal of School Health every day more than 2,000 American adolescents smoke their first cigarette and a proportionate number of Canadian adolescents equally do the same.
Over the lifetimes of these children, a significant number will die.
Twenty-five per cent of the teenagers who start smoking today will eventually die from diseases caused by this addiction.
This Government must accept the responsibility for supporting programs that will prevent our children from becoming addicted to nicotine and being lifetime smokers.
This is the Government's responsibility because smoking does not just pose health hazards to smokers themselves, it also puts non-smokers at risk because of the negative effects of secondhand smoke. Therefore, smoking is not just a personal health problem, it is also a social public health problem.
As a social public health problem, and in the interest of the common good, there are grounds for the Government to intervene to try to protect non-smokers from the ill effects of cigarette smoke.
Research has shown that the spouses and children of smokers have increased risk of serious health problems. One study found that children whose parents smoke have much higher rates of respiratory illness such as colds, influenza, and pneumonia and reduced lung capacity.
Of particular importance to the Bill we are now debating is the following statistics reported by the Canadian Health and Welfare study. A non-smoker who is exposed to secondhand smoke in the workplace for 20 years suffers the same negative effects as someone who has smoked 10 cigarettes a day for 20 years.
This is not only totally unfair to non-smokers, it is almost criminal. As a medical doctor, I am appalled that this Government has stalled so long before introducing amendments to a Bill which is so obviously vital to the welfare of Canadians.
There are also adverse economic effects of cigarette smoking. It is society that pays when a person is ill, is absent from work, or dies young and leaves dependants. Depending on the country, the direct health cost of dealing with smoking-related illness varies from 3 per cent to 5 per cent of all health care costs.
Health and Welfare Canada has estimated that the cost associated with smoking is twice as high as the revenue from tobacco taxation. The Health and Welfare study found that the economic costs of tobacco use in terms of mortality, disability, fire damage, direct hospitalization and physicians' fees is over $7 billion compared
June 26, 1989

with only approximately $4 billion in economic revenue from the tobacco industry.
It seems to me that most people would welcome this law banning smoking in the workplace except in designated areas. It has been enthusiastically supported by groups such as the Canadian Lung Association, the Non-Smokers' Rights Association, the Canadian Cancer Society, Physicians for a Smoke Free Canada, the Canadian Council on Smoking and Health and the Public Service Alliance of Canada.
Finally, I must point out that this Government does not have a good record when it comes to implementing legislation regulating smoking and tobacco. As noted in The Globe and Mail today, this Government allowed the tobacco industry to succeed in its lobby to remove two fundamental recommendations from the Tobacco Products Control Regulations, regulations which were to provide a serious warning system for tobacco.
First, this Government removed the requirement that every tobacco package should display messages identifying tobacco as addictive.
Second, the Government also removed the requirement that packages have an arrow circle display symbol which would draw attention to the risks of smoking.
This has seriously weakened the Tobacco Products Control Regulations and shows us that this Government cannot be trusted and that we must be careful to ensure that the Government takes its responsibilities to the citizens of Canada more seriously. It is obvious that the Non-smokers' Health Act is one that is necessary to help protect the good health of Canadians and to alleviate some of the negative and economic aspects of smoking.
With this new Act, hopefully the Government can redeem itself and show the people that truly the safety of Canadians is paramount and never can be subservient to the interests of the tobacco industry.

Mr. Speaker, I join with my colleagues and say it is a pleasure to participate in this debate. What becomes very clear is that this Bill is indeed a victory of parliamentary reform.
Non-smokers' Health Act
The Non-smokers' Health Act, known as Bill C-204 in the last Parliament, was a victory for the role of Private Members. It was the first controversial Private Members' Bill selected as a votable item to succeed its passage through the House of Commons. Its eventual passage was certainly a testament to the determination of its mover, Lynn McDonald from the constituency of Broad-wood-Greenwood. It was her incredible work that focused on the need to change the attitude of Canadians toward smoking, to show parliamentary leadership in terms of what could be done to clean up the Non-smokers' Health Act.
What we are debating today is a reflection of the success of that Private Members' Bill and indicates the diligence of the health community, particularly the Non-Smokers' Rights Association, the Canadian Medical Association, the Canadian Cancer Society and the Canadian Lung Association. There are other groups and hundreds of thousands of individuals who became involved in attempting to move parliamentarians to take action on this very, very critical issue.
I must say the willingness of back-benchers from all sides of the House, members of the New Democratic Party, Liberal and Conservative Parties, set aside partisan differences in moving that Private Members' Bill through. They voted for a cleaner environment and voted against the work of the tobacco lobby which if it had had its way would have us all smoking and smoking as much as we possibly could. That is a testament to how successful this place can be. All Members of Parliament deserve to be commended, those who voted in favour I might add, because there were still some who bowed to the pressure of the tobacco lobby and voted against a smoke-free workplace, if you can imagine, Mr. Speaker.
In the intervening months we have seen unanimous support for this initiative and now it seems incredibly Draconian to think that Members wanted to encourage people to smoke and encourage young people to begin the practice.
Unfortunately, the Bill did not emerge from the House unscathed. During very often acrimonious committee review, sections of the Bill were reworked and redrafted without the guidance of those who knew what elements were needed for the law to be enforceable. As a result, the Bill was more of a statement of principle than a framework for regulation. We all remember that

June 26, 1989
Non-smokers' Health Act
Bill C-204 received Royal Assent almost a year ago, yet it has never been proclaimed. It has not been enforced. It has never been able to become an act of law because administrators felt that it was unproclaimable until rewritten in a more enforceable framework. Fair enough. We are seeing the results of that effort today.
Earlier this year the Department of Labour, through the initiative of the Minister, entered into discussions with various employers, employee groups, health groups and, I suspect from recent news, tobacco interests and we worked the Non-smokers' Health Act into the version before us today. In the process a few changes were made to the principles involved but essentially preserved the integrity of the Act. Whereas Bill C-204, Lynn McDonald's Bill, gave workers the right to a smoke-free workplace, Bill C-27 before us imposes on employers the responsibility to ensure a smoke-free workplace for their workers. Those and other changes go to show that there is more than one legislative way to skin a cat.
What we know in the context of this legislation is that for more than a generation smoking kills people. I do not think there is any other way to put it. If you smoke excessively, chances are that you will die prematurely and that smoking will cause illnesses that every year lead to the death of many people. The most recent statistics- almost unbelievable-show that 35,000 Canadians die prematurely each year from diseases caused by tobacco smoke and illnesses caused by tobacco smoke.
We have only recently learned that the number of deaths caused by involuntary smoking, breathing the air which contains second-hand smoke, causes deaths as well. Last week the Environmental Protection Agency in the United States reported that environmental tobacco smoke was the greatest source of indoor air pollution in the U.S. Obviously, the same situation would apply to our own country. It is also reported that second-hand smoke was the greatest source of exposure to carcinogens. In other words, second-hand smoke exposed nonsmokers to more cancer-causing chemicals than any other aspect in their daily lives. I do not know if you are aware of it, Mr. Speaker, but there are 32,000 chemical agents in tobacco smoke, over 50 have been identified as likely carcinogens.
Health and Welfare has provided us with estimates that 330 Canadians die each year from lung cancers caused by breathing tobacco smoke-contaminated air in the workplace. This means that every year on average 330 Canadians die because people around them smoke. They do not, but the fact that there is smoke in the workplace causes 330 people to die.
We can all be very proud because this Bill, once it passes, will save the lives of at least 330 people every year. Bill C-27 flows out of Private Members' Bill C-204 introduced by Lynn McDonald.
There are a number of items I wish to refer to specifically, and one is the whole idea of a designated smoking room. Under the previous Bill, common carriers would have had to provide a separate room for smokers. Now they need only to set aside a separate area. That is essentially the situation that exists on airlines and buses now, as only a few rows of seats are made smoking seats, but the second-hand smoke still affects non-smoking passengers and employees on common carriers. I have a number of questions I want to put to the Minister on that issue in Committee of the Whole. As a matter of fact, to move this matter expeditiously, I should wait and make those comments and raise those questions during Committee of the Whole stage.
With that, I want to say that it is a delight to participate in this debate. All of us are concerned when we see young people encouraged to smoke by their peers or by advertising. We have taken steps in another way to pull back on those kinds of initiatives. I hope, through this legislation and related legislation, that we can encourage people not to smoke or to stop smoking. We should encourage people to rethink what the tobacco lobby has been successful in encouraging them to think, and that has been to remove some of the impact of the warning on cigarette packages. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to speak on Bill C-13, the Nordion and Theratronics Divestiture Authorization Act. It is something in which I have a great deal of interest. I do not believe that the privatization of these two companies is similar to a normal privatization which the Government would carry out. These are two very special companies. I believe the Government would be making a very severe mistake if it proceeded with the privatization of these companies, and I will relate why I feel this way.
In order to put my views across, it is very important to go back to the founding of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited and to the beginning of the nuclear industry in Canada. It began approximately in 1947 when the NRX reactor was developed in the Chalk River laboratories. Very soon thereafter, we had radio isotopes. These radio isotopes became very important in the treatment of cancer. When AECL was formed in 1952, it was logical that a branch of AECL called Commercial Products would become a separate division of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited. Thereafter AECL and Commercial Products continued to develop their technology for fighting cancer in Canada and eventually throughout the
Nordion and Theratronics
world, becoming more and more dependent upon the Cobalt-60 isotope. This became a world famous treatment.
With respect to that, Commercial Products, which in the early 1970s became two divisions, has developed most of the world's supply of Cobalt-60. AECL has secured a large portion of the world market for industrial units in fighting cancer and in the utilization of Cobalt-60. AECL has provided 71 of the 132 units in operation in the world today.
In the late 1970s, Commercial Products, because of its success and because of the fact that it was entering into the Medical Products Division and having some difficulty in marketing these newer products, Medical Products was split into two different groups. The company which dealt with the radio isotope and Cobalt-60 became the Radio Chemical Company. The unprofitable ventures into medical accelerators resulted in the formation of the Medical Products Division of AECL which looked after the accelerator work, the Cobalt therapy, the medical simulator treatment, planning and manufacture. After it was split off, these accelerators, treatment and therapy units became profitable.
So we have as recently as last year the two divisions, Radio Chemical and the Medical Products Division of AECL, being profitable. In fact, the Radio Chemical Company accounted for 80 per cent of the net income of AECL, the most profitable aspect of AECL. This should count for a great deal because we have heard from this Government that it wants the nuclear energy industry in Canada to thrive, to grow and to be solid. They want it to be secure and they want the people in Canada to have confidence in this industry.
In spite of this rhetoric, the Government has done absolutely nothing to secure these results in Canada. It is reducing the money that is being put into AECL and being put into the Atomic Energy Control Board which regulates the atomic energy industry in Canada. The Atomic Energy Control Board in fact has said in committee that it needs 100 per cent more funding if it is going to do the necessary supervisory work in the nuclear industry, if it is going to fulfil its obligations to find final depositories for high-level nuclear waste and for the other very important jobs that it must do.

June 26, 1989
Nordion and Theratronics
Therefore we have these two arms of AECL as recently as last year: the Medical Products Division which became profitable, and the Radio Chemical Company which accounted for 80 per cent of the net income of AECL.
What did this Government do? It decided that it would break these two divisions away from AECL. It put the two divisions under the Canada Development Investment Corporation and changed the names from Radio Chemical Company and Medical Products Division to Nordion and Theratronics, two entirely different corporations divested completely from AECL.
I mentioned earlier the reduced role of the Atomic Energy Control Board. I would like to talk about the problems within AECL itself. AECL was told by this Government: "We are going to cut back your budget. We want you to get into new areas. We want you to develop new technology." AECL has done that. There have been a lot of spinoffs from AECL which can be spun off into the private sector.
It would be unreasonable to say that all of the new technology that AECL has developed should be kept in AECL or should be kept in a separate Crown corporation. To do that would be asking the private sector to fund AECL and to be in competition with them. That would be highly unfair. There are a lot of companies that could be spun off.
The fact is that AECL has done what the Government has asked it to do. The only requirement that I would make to the Government is that when it splits off these areas from AECL and there are technological breakthroughs, that they at least put the money back into AECL. It is AECL technology that has led to these developments. If it wants AECL to look after itself, the Government cannot on the one hand say: "You have got to sell off these profitable arms", and on the other "put the money into the consolidated revenue account."
That being the case, generally I would say that new technology developed within AECL should be spun off into the private sector. However I make exceptions in the cases of Nordion and Theratronics because these are two unique companies. They deal first in health-related matters. They deal in matters that have been under the arm of AECL for many years. In fact, Radio Chemical, the radio isotopes and the Cobalt-60 technologies go
back to before the actual coming into being in 1952 of AECL itself.
AECL is dependent for 80 per cent of its net income on Nordion and its predecessor branches. If those two companies are spun off, AECL will not be able to rely on that income from them. In addition to not being able to rely on the funding, AECL will not be given the sale price of the two companies. It is estimated that $150 million will be brought in for the sale of Nordion and that Theratronics will bring between $50 million and $70 million. As far as we know, that money will go into the Consolidated Revenue account. AECL is going to lose its source of income year after year and will not be the recipient of the sale price of these two very important companies.
The Government believes, of course, that it can blunt any criticism about the sale of these two companies by taking them away from AECL before the actual sale and putting them in the Canada Development Investment Corporation. It did so to try to make these sales more palatable. The problem is that that cannot change the facts. These two companies are very important to AECL, they are very important to the future of AECL and they are very important, through the future of AECL, to the health of the nuclear industry in Canada.
Whatever your feelings about the nuclear industry, it is going to stay. We are not going to spend the billions of dollars in Ontario, New Brunswick and Quebec which would be needed to replace the nuclear reactors which exist and are providing that power. First and foremost, we must ensure that our nuclear industry is healthy. We keep it healthy by properly financing the umbrella that looks after the technology of our industry, that being AECL, and we make sure that our supervisory branch, the Atomic Energy Control Board, is properly supervised.
There is another reason why we should not be selling Nordion. That is,because Nordion has now developed the technology for irradiated food and they can sell this technology throughout the world. The problem is that there is a great deal of concern about irradiated food, not only in Canada but in countries throughout the world. There is a great deal of work to be done to ensure that this technology is further enhanced and is developed to remove the concern.
June 26, 1989

We know that the major problem with nuclear products is the concern of the public. It does not matter how good the technology is or how acceptable the product is, if we continually have to deal with apprehension by the public the nuclear industry in Canada is going to be inhibited, it is going to be a problem for government and is going to be a problem for the country. We must have the technology necessary to assure that irradiated food is brought within the realm of acceptance of the Canadian public, not through jingles or through public indoctrination but through fact and acceptance through the normal channels.
Canada and Nordion are so far ahead of the rest of the world in this technology that if we sell Nordion and its irradiated food technology, a private company could get its money back without doing any further research in this field. It could absolutely milk the technology for which the citizens of this country have paid over the last 37 years and we would be the losers. The world would be the loser. The countries where spoilage and bacteria of food supplies are a problem would be the losers. The Third World would be a very severe loser. We are playing with benefits which will come ultimately not only to Canada but to all mankind. If we can develop this technology it will be a source of tranquility for the world in general.
If there is no further technology, we will not have that assurance and we will also lose the edge that Canada has in this very important technology. Most important, we are playing with the health of Canadians and all citizens of the world. These are health-related companies. There is nothing that says we have to abandon every Crown corporation we ever had. There has to be some logic, some responsibility when dealing with the privatization of Crown corporations. Surely to heavens, companies that deal in products which affect the health of Canadians and people throughout the world must be kept under the federal umbrella to ensure that the technology dealt with is brought to a stage acceptable to Canadians.
The Government says that it handed out irradiated cookies to children and they could not taste the difference. What kind of an experiment is that? What kind of an assurance is that? If those parents knew that their children were eating those irradiated cookies there would be one heck of an outcry. The Government has not been able to say which children ate those irradiated cookies, but that is not the way in which the Government
Nordion and Theratronics
of Canada is going to be able to sell irradiated food to this country.
It is vital that the Government keep this technology within the framework of a Crown corporation or agency so that it can maintain the development, so that this technology will not be aborted and will not be commercialized by a private company in order to make a fast profit, thereby scaring the rest of the world and making this technology forever taboo. This is vital, Mr. Speaker. It is absolutely vital that the Government maintain the technology.
We have been told that the Government cannot retain the technology in Nordion because Nordion is under AECL and you know how long it takes for AECL to make any decisions. Well, it is the Government that takes the time in making decisions. If the Government wanted to make decisions more quickly with respect to Nordion and Theratronics, it could do so through its own actions. It does not have to pass any legislation, it does not have to coerce the business community, it does not have to frighten the Canadian public, it can do it through its own operations, its own management facilities, through a more efficient administration. It does not need to get rid of the company.
Some say that if the private sector is involved in Nordion we have a better chance to raise capital. Who is going to give the capital to AECL to replace the money it is losing if Nordion and Theratronics are privatized? The Government says that it wants a healthy nuclear industry in which the people of Canada have confidence. It is doing the opposite by privatizing these two very important and very lucrative Crown corporations.
I ask the Government to reconsider the privatization of these two corporations. I hope that second reading will be all we will be able to attain before we adjourn for the summer in order to give the Government the opportunity to rethink what I think would be a very serious mistake, that being the privatization of Nordion and Theratronics.
